card.headline: Alert sheep grazing together with the flock
card.look: A healthy sheep stays with the flock, grazes or chews cud calmly, and has bright eyes, pink eyelids, firm pellet droppings and a clean, even fleece or coat. It gets up quickly when you approach and moves freely on all four legs.
card.action: Watch your flock for a few minutes every morning and evening, and take a closer look at any sheep that is not behaving like the others.

detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy sheep looks, sounds and behaves like. Most illnesses in sheep first show as small changes from normal: a sheep standing alone, eating less, or passing soft droppings. Sheep are prey animals and naturally hide pain and weakness, so they often look fine until they are quite sick. If you know what normal looks like for your own flock, you will spot problems early, when treatment is cheaper and more likely to work.
detail.cause: Good health in sheep comes from a few basics working together. The first is good nutrition: enough grass, hay or browse, clean water at all times, and the right minerals, especially salt, calcium and phosphorus. The rumen (the large first stomach where microbes break down grass) needs a steady supply of fibre. That is why healthy sheep spend many hours a day grazing and many more chewing cud. Cud is food brought back up from the rumen to be chewed again. The second basic is control of parasites. Internal worms, especially the blood-sucking barber's pole worm (Haemonchus), and external parasites such as ticks, lice, keds and mange mites, steal blood and nutrients. The third is protection from infectious disease through vaccination, quarantine of new animals and clean housing. The fourth is low stress: dry, well-ventilated shelter, shade, gentle handling and not overcrowding. When all these are in place, the sheep's immune system can fight off the germs it meets every day, the rumen works smoothly, and the animal grows, breeds, lambs and produces wool or meat well.
spread: Good health spreads through a flock when the whole group is fed, watered and managed well, because sheep share pasture, water troughs and housing.
Disease and parasites usually enter a healthy flock through newly bought sheep, borrowed rams, or animals mixing at markets, shared grazing and communal watering points.
Contaminated pasture is a major trigger: worm eggs passed in dung hatch into larvae on wet grass, so worm problems often rise during and just after the long and short rains.
Sudden changes in feed, such as moving hungry sheep onto lush grass or giving too much grain, upset the rumen microbes and can trigger bloat, acidosis or enterotoxaemia (a clostridial toxin disease).
Wet, dirty, crowded or poorly ventilated housing encourages foot rot, pneumonia and skin problems, while very hot weather without shade causes heat stress.
Long dry seasons with poor pasture weaken body condition and immunity, making sheep more likely to fall sick when the rains return.
detail.atRisk: Every sheep benefits from a daily check, but some need closer attention. Young lambs in their first weeks are fragile and can go downhill within hours from cold, hunger, diarrhoea or pneumonia. Weaned lambs and young sheep under a year are most affected by worms because their immunity is still building. Pregnant ewes in late pregnancy and ewes in early lactation have high nutrient needs and are at risk of pregnancy toxaemia and milk fever. Rams can lose condition during the breeding season. Wool breeds such as Merino, Corriedale and Hampshire Down are more prone to heat stress and fly strike when fleece is long and dirty, while hair sheep such as Red Maasai and Dorper tend to cope better with heat; Red Maasai are known for relatively good tolerance of worms, though they are not immune. Flocks on wet, heavily grazed pasture during the rains, zero-grazed flocks fed cut grass from wet areas, and pastoral flocks that mix at watering points and markets all face extra risks.

early: The sheep stays with the flock, follows the others, and moves away calmly but quickly when approached; sheep are herd animals and a sheep alone is a warning sign.
Eyes are bright, clear and alert, with no tears, crust or cloudiness, and ears are held up and move in response to sounds.
The inside of the lower eyelid is pink to red, which shows enough red blood cells; check this by gently pulling down the lower lid.
Rectal temperature is between about 38.5 and 40 °C; it can sit near the top of this range on a hot afternoon or after the sheep has been chased.
Droppings are firm, dark, separate pellets that hold their shape; on very lush pasture they may clump a little, but there should be no watery scour or dirty tail.
The sheep chews cud for several hours each day, often while lying down, and you can see a rhythmic chewing and occasional swallowing and bringing up of the next cud.
The left side of the belly looks well filled but not tight or drum-like, and if you press your fist there you can feel the rumen move roughly one to two times a minute.
Breathing at rest is quiet and even, roughly 12 to 20 breaths a minute in cool weather, with no cough, nasal discharge or open-mouth breathing.
Fleece is even, dry and without bare patches, or the hair coat is smooth and shiny; the skin underneath is pink and clean, with no lice, keds, ticks or scabs.
The sheep walks evenly on all four feet, with no limping, and the feet smell clean, not rotten; the ewe's udder is soft, even and not hot or lumpy.
advanced: A sheep standing alone, lagging behind the flock, or lying down when others are grazing is often the first sign of illness.
Not eating, not chewing cud, or a dull, droopy head and ears can mean fever, pain or a rumen problem.
Pale pink or white eyelids point to anaemia, most often from barber's pole worm in Kenya, and need prompt action.
A temperature above about 40.5 °C suggests fever from infection, while a temperature below about 38 °C in a weak sheep is serious and can mean shock or a dying animal.
Soft, sloppy or watery droppings, a dirty back end, or no droppings at all show gut trouble.
A swollen left side, grinding teeth, kicking at the belly or straining are signs of pain or bloat.
Fast or laboured breathing at rest in cool weather, coughing, or a thick discharge from the nose suggests pneumonia.
Bottle jaw (a soft swelling under the jaw), limping, wool loss, constant scratching, or a swollen, hot udder all need closer checking.

lookalikes.name: Normal heat panting
lookalikes.howToTell: On hot afternoons, especially in wool breeds, healthy sheep may breathe fast with their mouths slightly open and seek shade. If they recover within an hour or so once in shade with water, eat normally and have a normal temperature in the cool of the evening, this is normal. Fast breathing in cool weather, or a sheep that does not settle in shade, is not normal.

lookalikes.name: Resting and cud chewing
lookalikes.howToTell: Healthy sheep lie down for long periods to chew cud, often in a group. They lie on their chest with legs tucked, heads up, chewing, and get up quickly when disturbed. A sick sheep lies apart from the others, may lie flat on its side, does not chew, and is slow or unwilling to rise.

lookalikes.name: Soft droppings on fresh pasture
lookalikes.howToTell: When sheep move onto lush rain-season grass, droppings often become softer and clumped for a few days while the rumen adjusts. The sheep stays bright and keeps eating. Watery scour, a strong smell, blood or mucus, a dull sheep, or soft dung lasting more than a few days needs investigating, often for worms or coccidiosis.

lookalikes.name: A ewe about to lamb
lookalikes.howToTell: A ewe close to lambing may separate herself, paw the ground, lie down and get up, and eat less. This is normal behaviour. If she strains for more than about 30 minutes to an hour without progress, seems weak, wobbly or blind, or stops eating in late pregnancy before any signs of labour, call the vet, as this can be a difficult birth or pregnancy toxaemia.

detail.diagnosis: A home health check takes a few minutes per sheep and is the best tool you have. Start by watching the flock from a distance before you disturb them: who is alone, who is not eating, who is lying differently, who is limping or coughing. Then catch and gently restrain one sheep at a time, against a wall or in a small pen. Temperature: use a digital thermometer, lubricate the tip with petroleum jelly or a little cooking oil, lift the tail and insert it gently into the rectum about 3–5 cm, angled so the tip touches the side wall. Hold it until it beeps or for about one minute. Normal is about 38.5–40 °C. Take temperatures in the cool of the morning if you can, and check a few healthy sheep for comparison. Clean the thermometer with soap and water and disinfectant after each animal. Eyelids: pull down the lower eyelid with your thumb and look at the colour. Red to pink is good; pale pink or white means anaemia. Extension officers in some areas use the FAMACHA card, a colour chart for this check, and it helps decide which sheep need deworming. Body condition: feel along the backbone behind the last rib. If the spine is sharp and you can easily feel between the bones, the sheep is thin; if you can barely feel the bones under a firm pad, it is in good condition; if you cannot feel them at all, it may be too fat. Most farmers use a 1 to 5 scale, aiming for about 2.5 to 3.5 depending on stage of production. Also check: rumen fill and movement on the left flank, breathing rate by counting flank movements for one minute, nose and eyes for discharge, the jaw for bottle jaw swelling, mouth and lips for scabs, skin and fleece for parasites, the udder and teats, the feet between the claws for heat, swelling or a rotten smell, and the back end for scour. Write down the sheep's ear tag or name, the date and what you found. These records help your vet a great deal if a problem appears later.
firstSteps: Watch the whole flock every morning and evening for at least a few minutes, looking for any sheep that is alone, dull, not eating or not chewing cud.
Give every sheep access to clean, fresh water all day, and check troughs and containers daily for dirt, algae or dead insects.
Provide shade and shelter that is dry, clean and well ventilated, with enough space so sheep are not crowded.
Make sure salt and a sheep mineral lick or mineral mix are available, especially in the dry season and for pregnant and milking ewes.
Keep a simple health notebook with each sheep's tag, weight or condition score, vaccinations, deworming dates, lambings and any illness.
Separate any sheep that looks unwell into a clean, quiet pen with water, shade and good feed, and check its temperature and eyelids.
Keep newly bought sheep apart from your flock for at least two to three weeks and watch them closely before mixing.
Call your vet or animal health officer early if a sheep has a fever, pale eyelids, scour, breathing trouble, or stops eating, rather than waiting until it goes down.
detail.vetTreatment: Routine vet care keeps a healthy flock healthy. A good relationship with your local vet or County veterinary staff means faster help when something goes wrong. Typical routine care includes a vaccination plan suited to your area. This often covers clostridial diseases such as enterotoxaemia (pulpy kidney) and tetanus, and sheep and goat pox. It also includes PPR (peste des petits ruminants, often called goat plague), usually given through government campaigns. Rift Valley fever vaccination may be advised by the authorities when there is a risk of outbreaks after heavy rains. Other vaccines may be recommended depending on local disease risk. The vet can help you plan deworming. Instead of deworming every sheep on a fixed calendar, many vets now advise targeted deworming: treat sheep with pale eyelids, poor condition or scour, and use faecal egg counts (a lab test counting worm eggs in dung) to check whether a dewormer still works. This slows down dewormer resistance, which is a growing problem in Kenya. The vet can also advise on tick, lice and mange control, foot trimming and foot baths, castration and tail docking where practised, ram fertility checks before mating, and feeding plans for pregnant ewes. All medicines, including dewormers, acaricides and antibiotics, should be used as directed by a vet or on the label. Respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time after treatment before milk or meat is safe to use or sell. Antibiotics should only be used when a vet decides they are needed, to avoid antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs.
prevention: Follow a vaccination programme agreed with your vet or County Veterinary Officer, and take part in government PPR and other campaigns when they reach your area.
Control worms by rotating pastures, avoiding grazing very short grass in wet seasons, checking eyelids regularly, and deworming based on need and vet advice rather than guesswork.
Control ticks, lice, keds and mange with regular checks and correct use of acaricides, following label withdrawal periods.
Feed enough good-quality forage all year, conserve hay or silage for the dry season, and provide salt and minerals so sheep do not develop deficiencies.
Make feed changes gradually over about one to two weeks, especially when moving to lush pasture or introducing grain or concentrates.
Keep housing raised, dry and well ventilated, remove wet bedding and dung often, and avoid overcrowding to reduce foot rot, pneumonia and skin disease.
Quarantine new animals, avoid sharing rams with unknown flocks, and limit contact with other flocks at markets and communal watering points where possible.
Trim feet when needed, shear wool breeds at the right time to reduce heat stress and fly strike, and handle sheep calmly to reduce stress.
detail.impact: A healthy flock is a profitable flock. Sheep that are well fed, free of heavy worm burdens and protected by vaccination grow faster, reach market weight sooner and fetch better prices. Healthy ewes conceive more readily, have fewer abortions, and raise stronger lambs with more milk. On many Kenyan smallholder farms sheep are a savings account, sold for school fees, emergencies or festive seasons. Losing even one or two animals to a preventable problem is a real financial blow. Daily checks cost nothing but a few minutes, and catching a problem early usually means cheaper treatment, less weight loss and fewer deaths. Poor health shows up as slow growth, thin ewes, lamb deaths, lower wool quality, extra spending on drugs and vet visits, and sheep sold cheaply because they look poor. Good records and a routine health plan also make it easier to sell breeding stock and to show buyers your flock is well managed.
detail.humanHealth: Healthy-looking sheep can still carry some germs that infect people, such as brucellosis and Q fever (spread mainly through birth fluids, afterbirths and raw milk), and orf (scabby mouth), which can cause sores on hands. Wash your hands with soap after handling sheep, wear gloves when helping at lambing or handling afterbirths, bury or burn afterbirths and aborted lambs, and boil milk before drinking it. Always respect withdrawal periods after any treatment so drug residues do not end up in milk or meat.
detail.outlook: A flock that is checked daily, well fed, given clean water, vaccinated and protected from parasites can stay productive for many years, and most problems that do arise can be caught early. No management system prevents every illness, and weather, local disease outbreaks and dewormer resistance can still cause setbacks. Farmers who know what normal looks like for their own sheep usually notice trouble a day or two sooner. That head start often makes the difference between a quick recovery and a lost animal. Building a good relationship with your local vet and keeping simple records will improve the outlook for your flock over time.

faqs.q: How often should I check my sheep?
faqs.a: Look at the whole flock at least twice a day, ideally in the morning before they go out and in the evening when they come back. This only takes a few minutes. Do a closer hands-on check of each sheep, including eyelids, body condition and feet, about every two to four weeks. Check more often during the rains when worms are high, in late pregnancy, and in young lambs.

faqs.q: What temperature means my sheep has a fever?
faqs.a: A normal sheep's rectal temperature is about 38.5 to 40 °C. A reading above about 40.5 °C, especially in a sheep that is dull or not eating, usually means fever and you should call your vet. Remember that a sheep that has been chased or is standing in hot sun can read a little high, so let it rest in shade and recheck. A low reading below about 38 °C in a weak sheep is an emergency.

faqs.q: How do I know if my sheep is too thin or just a small breed?
faqs.a: Breed and size are different from condition. A small Red Maasai can be in excellent condition while a big Dorper can be thin. Feel along the backbone just behind the ribs. If the bones feel sharp and you can push your fingers easily between them, the sheep is thin whatever its size. If there is a firm, smooth cover of flesh over the bones, it is in good condition. Thin sheep should be checked for worms, teeth problems and poor feeding.

faqs.q: Why is one of my sheep standing alone?
faqs.a: Sheep feel safe in a group, so a sheep standing apart is often unwell, in pain, or about to lamb. Check its temperature, eyelid colour, droppings, breathing and feet, and see whether it is eating and chewing cud. If it is a ewe close to lambing, watch her closely. If you cannot find an obvious reason, or she does not rejoin the flock within a few hours, call your vet.

faqs.q: Should I deworm all my sheep every few months?
faqs.a: Routine blanket deworming of every sheep on a fixed schedule is no longer recommended by many vets, because it speeds up dewormer resistance. A better approach is to check eyelids, body condition and droppings, deworm the sheep that need it, and ask your vet about faecal egg counts. Your vet may still advise strategic treatments at certain times, such as before or after the rains. Always follow label withdrawal periods.

faqs.q: Do healthy sheep really need minerals and vitamins?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Kenyan pastures, especially in the dry season, are low in phosphorus and other minerals, and sheep on dry or poor feed can also run short of vitamins such as A and E. Shortages show up slowly as poor growth, weak lambs, poor fertility and chewing on bones or soil. Salt and a good sheep mineral lick or mix should always be available. Ask your vet or extension officer what suits your area. Avoid mineral mixes made for cattle or poultry unless a vet confirms they are safe for sheep, because sheep are sensitive to too much copper.

products.role: As part of a balanced mineral programme, DCP-18 can help supply calcium and phosphorus for strong bones, growth and milk production, especially for growing lambs and pregnant or milking ewes on dry-season or phosphorus-poor pasture. Use it alongside salt, good forage and vet or extension advice on the right mineral mix for sheep.

During long dry seasons, or when sheep are housed on dry feed with little green grass, AD3E can help prevent vitamin A, D3 and E shortages that affect fertility, lamb vigour and stiff lamb problems. Use it as a nutritional support under vet or extension guidance, not as a replacement for good forage.

healthy.imagePrompt: A small flock of healthy sheep, mixing Dorper and Red Maasai types, grazing together on green pasture in the Kenyan highlands in soft morning light, with bright eyes, clean even coats, alert ears and one sheep lying down chewing cud.
healthy.seoDescription: Learn what a healthy sheep looks like: normal temperature 38.5–40 °C, pink eyelids, firm pellets, cud chewing and a simple daily check for Kenyan farmers.

card.headline: Raised lumps and scabs on woolless skin
card.look: Sheep with fever, watery eyes and a runny nose develop red spots that turn into firm, raised lumps and then dark scabs. These show on the face, ears, under the tail, the udder and inside the thighs. Lambs may struggle to breathe and die quickly.
card.action: Isolate the sick sheep, stop all movement of animals on and off the farm, and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, because sheep pox is a notifiable disease.

aka: Capripox (with goat pox and lumpy skin disease)
detail.summary: Sheep pox is a highly contagious viral disease of sheep. It causes fever, skin lumps that turn into scabs, eye and nose discharge, and often pneumonia. It can kill many lambs and newly introduced or exotic breeds, and it damages skins and slows growth in survivors. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected case must be reported to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: Sheep pox is caused by the sheep pox virus. It belongs to the capripox group, which also includes goat pox virus and lumpy skin disease virus of cattle. In East Africa, many sheep pox and goat pox strains can infect both sheep and goats. The virus enters through the nose, mouth or broken skin. It multiplies, spreads through the blood and settles in the skin, the lining of the airways, the lungs and the gut. In the skin it kills cells and causes swelling, producing red spots that harden into raised lumps called nodules. These lumps die from the centre and form dark scabs. The same kind of damage in the windpipe and lungs makes breathing hard and opens the way for bacteria to cause pneumonia, which means infection of the lungs. Lambs and animals that have never met the virus have little defence. Their bodies can be overwhelmed, and they die from the virus itself or from bacterial infections that follow.
spread: Close contact between sick and healthy sheep, especially when they are crowded in a boma, pen, truck or market.
Breathing in droplets from the nose, mouth and eye discharge of infected sheep, particularly at night in shared housing.
Scabs that fall off sick animals contain large amounts of virus. They can remain infectious in pens, bedding, soil and wool for months, especially in shaded, dry places.
Contaminated items such as feeding troughs, water points, shearing tools, ropes, vehicles, clothing and boots.
Biting flies, such as stable flies, can carry the virus on their mouthparts from one animal to another.
Buying new sheep or goats from markets or neighbours without a quarantine period. Animals may carry the virus before they show signs.
Shared grazing, communal dips and watering points, and the movement of flocks in pastoral areas during drought or after the rains.
detail.atRisk: All ages of sheep can be infected, but young lambs suffer the most and die in the highest numbers. Exotic and improved breeds, such as Dorper, Merino and their crosses, are usually more severely affected than local breeds like Red Maasai and Blackhead Persian. Local breeds are not immune, especially if they have never been vaccinated. Animals that are new to an area, under stress, poorly fed, pregnant or carrying heavy worm burdens tend to get sicker. Outbreaks are more common where flocks mix: pastoral and semi-pastoral systems, livestock markets, communal grazing and watering points, and areas where animals move during drought. Fly numbers rise during and after the long and short rains, which can help spread the virus. Unvaccinated flocks in any farming system, including zero-grazing units that buy in stock, are at risk.

early: High fever. The sheep is dull, stands apart from the flock, and may stop eating and chewing the cud.
Watery eyes and swollen, puffy eyelids. The sheep may squint or keep its eyes half closed.
Clear, watery discharge from the nose, sometimes with sneezing or snorting.
Red, flat spots on skin with little or no wool: around the eyes, lips, nostrils, ears, under the tail, on the udder or scrotum, and inside the thighs.
Swollen lymph nodes, which are the small glands in front of the shoulder and below the ear. They feel like firm lumps under the skin.
Within a day or two, the red spots rise into firm, raised lumps that you can feel by running your hand over the skin, including under the wool.
advanced: Lumps become hard and dark in the centre, then turn into thick black or brown scabs that may crack and attract flies.
Nose discharge turns thick, yellow and sticky. It can crust around the nostrils and block breathing.
Fast, laboured or noisy breathing and coughing, which are signs of pneumonia.
Sores inside the mouth and on the tongue, causing drooling and refusal to eat.
Rapid weight loss and weakness. Some animals cannot get up.
Pregnant ewes may abort.
Lambs may die suddenly, sometimes before many skin lumps are seen.
Survivors are left with scars where scabs fell off, and the wool may break or come out in patches.

lookalikes.name: Orf (contagious ecthyma)
lookalikes.howToTell: Orf mainly causes crusty, cauliflower-like sores on the lips, muzzle, gums and teats, mostly in young lambs. Fever is usually mild, sheep rarely die unless they cannot suckle, and lumps do not spread over the whole body as in sheep pox. Orf can infect people's hands, which helps tell it apart.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR causes fever, eye and nose discharge and pneumonia, like sheep pox. However, it also causes mouth erosions with a bad smell and severe diarrhoea, and it often hits goats harder than sheep. It does not cause raised skin lumps all over the body. PPR is also notifiable, so report it either way.

lookalikes.name: Bluetongue
lookalikes.howToTell: Bluetongue causes fever, a swollen face and lips, mouth sores, sometimes a bluish tongue, and lameness with red bands above the hooves. It is spread by small biting midges in wet seasons. It does not produce the firm skin nodules and scabs typical of sheep pox.

lookalikes.name: Sheep scab (mange) or dermatophilosis (lumpy wool)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange causes intense itching, rubbing and wool loss, but no high fever or nose discharge. Dermatophilosis causes matted, crusty wool along the back after long wet spells. Sheep are usually still bright and eating, and there are no deep nodules or deaths in lambs.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will first examine the flock, looking at the pattern of skin lumps, fever, eye and nose discharge and breathing problems, and how many animals and which ages are affected. Because sheep pox is notifiable, the vet will take samples for laboratory confirmation. These usually include pieces of skin lumps, scabs, and blood taken during the fever stage. They are sent to a government laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete. Tests such as PCR, which detects the virus's genetic material, can confirm the virus and tell it apart from orf, PPR and other diseases. If a sheep dies, a post-mortem (an examination of the body after death) may show pox lesions in the windpipe, lungs, stomach and intestines. To help the vet, note when the first animal fell sick, how many are sick and how many have died, and the ages and breeds involved. Also record any recent purchases, market visits or shared grazing, and the vaccination history of the flock. Keep any dead animal covered and away from dogs and scavengers until the vet says what to do. Do not open it yourself.
firstSteps: Call your County Veterinary Officer or the nearest government veterinary office straight away. Report that you suspect sheep pox. This is required by law, and early reporting protects your neighbours' flocks too.
Separate sick sheep from healthy ones at once. Keep them in a shaded, well-ventilated pen away from other sheep and goats, and use separate feeding and watering equipment for them.
Stop all movement. Do not sell, buy, lend or take sheep or goats to market, grazing or watering points shared with other flocks until the vet advises you.
Give sick animals clean, fresh water and soft, palatable feed such as green fodder or good hay. Sheep with sore mouths may eat only soft feed.
Keep animals calm, dry and out of cold wind and hot sun, and handle them gently. Stress and chilling make pneumonia worse.
Gently wipe crusted discharge from the nose and eyes with a clean, damp cloth so the animal can breathe and see. Burn or bury the cloths afterwards.
Limit flies around the pens by removing wet bedding and dung regularly. Do not pick off scabs, because they are full of virus.
Wear an overall and boots that stay on your farm. Handle healthy animals before sick ones, and wash hands and boots after every visit. Ask visitors and traders to stay away.
Record each sick and dead animal with dates and signs. Do not give any drugs, sell animals, or slaughter sick sheep until a vet has examined the flock.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the sheep pox virus. Antibiotics do not cure the virus. Treatment aims to keep animals alive while their immune system fights the infection, and to control the bacterial infections that often follow. A vet may prescribe antibiotics, for example from the tetracycline or penicillin groups, to treat or prevent secondary pneumonia and infected skin sores. They may also prescribe anti-inflammatory drugs to ease fever and pain, and wound sprays or fly repellents to protect scabs. Only a vet should decide which drugs to use and how. Using antibiotics without a prescription, or stopping a course early, helps bacteria become resistant to drugs (antimicrobial resistance). This makes future infections harder to treat. Every drug has a withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment when meat and milk must not be eaten or sold. Follow the period the vet gives you exactly. Because the disease is notifiable, the veterinary authorities may put the farm and surrounding area under quarantine. They may also organise vaccination of healthy in-contact and neighbouring flocks (ring vaccination) and give instructions on disposing of carcasses and disinfecting pens. Recovery is slow. Skin lumps can take several weeks to heal, and very sick lambs may die despite good care.
prevention: Vaccinate. Kenya produces a live sheep and goat pox vaccine (KEVEVAPI), which is available through agrovets and veterinary offices and protects against the capripox strains found in the region. Ask your vet when to vaccinate and how often to repeat it, which in many flocks is yearly. Include lambs at the recommended age and all new stock.
Keep the vaccine cold and use it correctly. Live vaccines must stay in a cool box or fridge and be used soon after mixing. Vaccine that has been left in the sun may give no protection.
Quarantine every new sheep or goat for at least three weeks before it joins your flock. Watch it for fever, eye and nose discharge and skin lumps, and vaccinate it if its history is unknown.
Avoid markets, shared grazing, communal watering points and borrowing rams during an outbreak in your area. Follow any movement controls announced by the County Veterinary Officer.

Keep pens clean, dry and well ventilated, and avoid overcrowding in bomas. After an outbreak, remove and burn or bury bedding, scabs and wool, then clean and disinfect pens and equipment as your vet advises.
Control biting flies through good manure management, drainage of wet areas, and vet-approved fly control, especially during and after the long and short rains.
Keep the flock strong with good feeding, clean water, regular deworming and tick control. Well-nourished animals cope better with disease and respond better to vaccination.
Report any suspicious skin lumps early. Fast reporting allows ring vaccination and stops the virus spreading across a whole village or grazing area.
detail.impact: Sheep pox can be one of the most costly diseases a sheep farmer faces. In unvaccinated flocks, many lambs may die, wiping out a season's growth. Losses are often heavy in improved breeds such as Dorpers, which farmers have paid a lot for. Adults that survive lose weight, grow slowly and may abort, so the next lamb crop is smaller. Scars on the skin lower the value of hides and skins, and wool is damaged. During an outbreak, quarantine and movement restrictions can stop sales for weeks, just when a farmer may need cash for school fees or to buy feed. Whole markets may be closed. Spending rises on vet visits, treatment of secondary infections, labour for nursing and disinfection. In pastoral areas, where sheep are savings and security, an outbreak can quickly set a household back. Vaccination costs far less than these losses.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mainly on the animal's age, breed and immunity. Many adult sheep of local breeds recover, though healing of skin lumps and scabs can take several weeks and leaves scars. Lambs, exotic and improved breeds, and animals that develop pneumonia or stop eating have a much poorer outlook, and many may die. Good nursing, shade, water, soft feed and prompt vet treatment of secondary infections improve the chances. Sheep that recover usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity to sheep pox. Vaccinating the rest of the flock early in an outbreak can limit how many animals fall sick.

faqs.q: Can my goats and cattle catch sheep pox?
faqs.a: In East Africa, many sheep pox and goat pox strains can infect both sheep and goats, so treat goats on the same farm as at risk and include them in vaccination if your vet advises. Cattle get a related disease, lumpy skin disease, but sheep pox does not normally cause disease in cattle. Keep all species separate from sick sheep and follow your vet's guidance.

faqs.q: Can I vaccinate my healthy sheep when there is an outbreak?
faqs.a: Yes, vaccinating healthy and in-contact animals is often a key part of controlling an outbreak. The veterinary authorities may organise it in your area. Some animals may already be incubating the virus when vaccinated and still fall sick, so do not be discouraged if a few cases appear soon after. Always vaccinate under the guidance of a vet, and never vaccinate animals that are already sick unless the vet tells you to.

faqs.q: Can people catch sheep pox or get sick from eating the meat?
faqs.a: Sheep pox is not considered a disease of people. However, sick animals should never be slaughtered for sale. Moving carcasses, meat and skins can spread the virus to other flocks, and quarantine rules may forbid it. Any animal that has received drugs must also complete the withdrawal period before its meat or milk is used. Ask your County Veterinary Officer before slaughtering any animal from an affected flock.

faqs.q: Will a sheep that recovered get sheep pox again?
faqs.a: Sheep that recover usually have strong, long-lasting protection against the disease. Their scars remain, and they may have lost weight and condition, so give them good feeding to recover. New lambs and newly bought animals will not share that protection, so they still need vaccination.

faqs.q: How long will movement restrictions last on my farm?
faqs.a: This depends on the decision of the veterinary authorities. Restrictions usually stay until no new cases have appeared for a set period and the pens have been cleaned and disinfected. Movement restrictions mean you cannot sell, buy or move sheep and goats, or their skins, in or out of the quarantine area without permission. Breaking these rules is against the law and spreads the disease to other farmers. Stay in touch with your County Veterinary Officer for updates.

faqs.q: Are there home remedies or supplements that cure sheep pox?
faqs.a: No. Nothing given at home kills the virus. Good nursing really helps sheep survive: shade, clean water, soft feed, cleaning the nose and eyes, and keeping the animals calm. Any medicine, including for fever or secondary infection, should be prescribed by a vet. The most reliable protection is vaccinating your flock before the disease arrives.

card.headline: Swollen face, lips and drooling mouth
card.look: A dull, feverish sheep with puffy lips, muzzle and ears, drooling saliva and a red, sore mouth. Some sheep have a bluish-purple tongue, and many limp because the skin just above the hooves is red and painful.
card.action: Move sick sheep into shade, give them clean water and soft feed, keep them under cover from dusk to dawn, and call your vet to confirm the disease.

detail.summary: Bluetongue is a viral disease of sheep spread by tiny biting midges, not by direct contact between animals. It causes fever, swelling of the face and lips, a sore mouth, drooling and lameness. Only some sheep get the blue tongue the disease is named after. It matters because sick sheep stop eating, lose weight and wool, may abort, and some die. Outbreaks are common in the wet seasons, when midges breed in large numbers.
detail.cause: Bluetongue is caused by the bluetongue virus, an orbivirus. Many different types, called serotypes, exist around the world, and several circulate in East Africa. When an infected midge bites a sheep, the virus enters the blood and multiplies in the lining of small blood vessels. These damaged vessels leak fluid and bleed into the tissues. That leaking causes the swollen face, lips, ears and jaw. It also causes the red, raw areas in the mouth and the painful redness at the coronary band. The coronary band is the band of skin where the hoof meets the hairline. In severe cases, poor blood flow turns the tongue bluish-purple. The virus can also damage muscles, causing stiffness and reluctance to move, and damage the lungs, which leads to pneumonia. In pregnant ewes some strains cross to the unborn lamb. This can cause abortion or weak lambs born with brain defects. A sheep that recovers is usually protected against that serotype, but not always against other serotypes.
spread: The main route is the bite of infected Culicoides midges. These are tiny biting insects, smaller than mosquitoes, often called 'no-see-ums'.
Midges breed in wet mud, manure, rotting plant matter and the edges of ponds, dams and water troughs. Their numbers rise sharply during and after the long and short rains.
Midges feed mostly at dusk, through the night and at dawn, especially in warm, still, humid weather. Sheep kept outside at night are bitten most.
Cattle, goats and wild ruminants such as antelope can carry the virus, often without showing illness. Midges then carry it from these animals to sheep.
Wind can carry midges over long distances, so infection can arrive even if you have bought no new animals.
Reusing needles between animals can spread the virus by moving infected blood from one animal to the next.
Some strains pass from an infected ewe to her unborn lamb, and the virus can be present in the semen of infected rams.
Bluetongue does not spread by sheep touching, sharing feed or grazing together. Without midges, a sick sheep will not infect its flock-mates.
detail.atRisk: All sheep can be infected, but disease is usually most severe in improved and imported breeds and their crosses. These include wool breeds such as Merino and Corriedale, and many exotic meat breeds. Animals newly brought into an area where the virus circulates are especially at risk. Indigenous breeds such as Red Maasai and Blackhead Persian, and flocks raised for generations in the same area, often have mild or hidden infections because they have built up immunity. Young lambs from immune ewes are partly protected by antibodies in the first milk (colostrum) for their first few months. After that protection fades, they become at risk. Risk is highest in the rainy seasons and the warm weeks just after them. Flocks grazing near swamps, dams, irrigation schemes or river valleys are at higher risk, as are flocks kept in open bomas or left out overnight. In pastoral systems, sheep that share grazing and water with cattle, goats and wildlife are regularly exposed. Zero-grazed and semi-intensive flocks can also be hit when manure and wet bedding near the housing let midges breed.

early: High fever: the sheep feels hot, breathes fast and stands apart from the flock with its head down.
Loss of appetite and dullness. The sheep stops grazing or only nibbles soft feed.
Redness inside the mouth and on the gums, with heavy drooling and frothy saliva around the lips.
Clear nasal discharge that soon becomes thick and crusty around the nostrils.
Swelling of the lips, muzzle, face and ears. A soft, fluid-filled swelling may also appear under the jaw.
Watery eyes and reddened eye linings.
Stiffness or a slight limp, with the sheep reluctant to walk or keep up with the flock.
advanced: Raw sores and ulcers on the dental pad, gums, tongue and inside the cheeks. The mouth may smell bad.
A swollen, bluish-purple tongue that may hang out of the mouth. This is seen in only some sheep.
Clear lameness with a red or purple band at the top of the hooves. Some sheep kneel to graze or refuse to stand.
Marked weight loss and weakness from not eating and from muscle damage. The neck may be held twisted in some animals.
Laboured breathing, coughing and discharge from the nose, which are signs of pneumonia.
Diarrhoea, sometimes with blood, in a few severe cases.
Abortion in pregnant ewes, or lambs born weak, blind or unable to stand properly.
Weeks later, the wool may become weak and break, or fall out in patches (a 'wool break'). Hooves may develop rings or cracks as they grow out.

lookalikes.name: Orf (contagious ecthyma, sore mouth)
lookalikes.howToTell: Orf causes thick, crusty, wart-like scabs on the lips and nostrils, mostly in young lambs and kids. It spreads by contact. Fever and face swelling are usually mild, and lameness from the coronary band is uncommon. Orf can also infect people's hands, which bluetongue cannot.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR, goat plague)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR spreads quickly by contact. It often hits goats harder than sheep, with heavy eye and nose discharge, mouth sores, severe diarrhoea, pneumonia and many deaths within days. Face swelling and coronary band lameness are not typical. PPR is notifiable in Kenya, so report any suspicion to the County Veterinary Officer at once.

lookalikes.name: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)
lookalikes.howToTell: FMD causes fluid-filled blisters (vesicles) that burst in the mouth, between the claws and on the teats. It often affects cattle in the same area at the same time and spreads by contact. Sheep usually show mainly sudden lameness. The face swelling of bluetongue is not a feature. FMD is notifiable, so report it.

lookalikes.name: Footrot or foot abscess
lookalikes.howToTell: Footrot causes lameness with a foul-smelling, rotting area between the claws or under the hoof. There is no fever, face swelling or mouth sores, and the sheep usually keeps eating normally.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will suspect bluetongue from the season, the signs and the flock history. Clear pointers are a sore, swollen face, drooling, coronary band redness and lameness in the rainy season, with no sign of contact spread. The vet examines the mouth, feet, eyes and breathing and takes the temperature. Because PPR and foot-and-mouth disease can look similar and are notifiable, the vet will want to rule them out. To confirm bluetongue, blood is taken in a tube with anticoagulant (EDTA) and sent to a government or university veterinary laboratory. There, a PCR test detects the virus's genetic material and can identify the serotype. Blood tests for antibodies (ELISA) show whether the flock has been exposed. If a sheep dies, a post-mortem examination can show typical bleeding at the base of the main artery from the heart, muscle damage and fluid in the lungs. Tissue samples can then be tested. To help the vet, write down when the first sheep fell sick, and how many are sick or have died. Note their ages, breeds and pregnancy status. Record any recent purchases, the weather and rainfall, and whether your cattle or goats look unwell. Keep sick animals in a shaded pen close to where the vet can reach them.
firstSteps: Separate sick sheep into a calm, shaded, well-ventilated pen near water. They are not contagious to other sheep by contact, but they need rest and close watching.
Give plenty of clean, fresh water in a shallow container they can reach easily. Sheep with sore mouths and feet often stop drinking if water is far away or hard to reach.
Offer soft, palatable feed such as fresh soft grass, soaked hay, or a wet mash of bran or concentrate. Rough, stalky fodder hurts a sore mouth.
Keep the whole flock under a roof or in a closed shed from late afternoon until after sunrise, when midges bite most. Avoid grazing near swamps and dams at dusk and dawn.
Bed lame sheep on soft, dry ground or straw. Do not drive them long distances to grazing or water, because walking on sore feet and damaged muscles makes them worse.
Keep sheep out of direct sun as much as possible. Bright sunlight can worsen the damaged skin on the face and ears, and shade helps them cope with fever.
Do not give any medicine, including fever tablets or antibiotics, until your vet has examined the animals and prescribed treatment.

Record which animals are sick, their signs, and daily changes. Call your vet or the County Veterinary Officer, especially if you see many sick animals, deaths, abortions, or signs in goats and cattle too.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the bluetongue virus. Antibiotics do not cure bluetongue, because it is a virus. Treatment aims to ease pain and fever, prevent complications and help the body fight off the infection. A vet may prescribe an anti-inflammatory painkiller, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as meloxicam or flunixin. This reduces fever, swelling and pain, so the sheep is more willing to eat, drink and move. If the vet finds a secondary bacterial infection, such as pneumonia or badly infected mouth or foot sores, they may prescribe an antibiotic. These must be used only when truly needed, for the full course the vet sets, to limit antimicrobial resistance, which happens when bacteria stop responding to antibiotics. The vet may also advise on cleaning mouth sores, softening feed, giving fluids to dehydrated animals, and nursing lame sheep. Every drug used has a withdrawal period. This is the time you must wait after the last treatment before the animal's meat or milk can be sold or eaten. Ask your vet for the withdrawal period of each product and keep a written record. Expect recovery to be slow. Fever usually settles over several days, but mouth sores, lameness and weight loss can take weeks to improve. Badly affected sheep may need nursing for a long time. The vet will never give doses over the phone without examining the animals, and you should not copy doses from another farmer.
prevention: Vaccination is the most effective way to protect sheep where bluetongue is common. Vaccines must match the serotypes in your area, so ask your County Veterinary Officer or private vet which vaccines are available in Kenya and when to use them.
Vaccinate before the rains, when midges are fewest. Follow the vet's advice on pregnant ewes, because some live (modified) vaccines are not suitable in early pregnancy and can harm the unborn lamb.

House sheep at night, or bring them into a closed shed from dusk to dawn during the rainy seasons. This greatly cuts midge bites. Fine mesh screens or insecticide-treated netting on housing can help further.
Reduce midge breeding sites around the boma and sheds. Remove manure and wet bedding often, fix leaking troughs and pipes, fill or drain muddy patches, and keep the area around water points dry.
Where possible, graze sheep away from swamps, dams, river banks and irrigation channels in the evening and early morning.

Ask your vet about insect-repellent or insecticide pour-ons and sprays (usually synthetic pyrethroids) during high-risk months. These reduce bites but do not give complete protection, so use them alongside housing and vaccination.

Be careful when buying improved or exotic sheep to bring into an area where bluetongue occurs. Buy in the dry season, vaccinate them as advised by a vet, and house them at night while their immunity builds.
Use a new, clean needle for each animal when injecting or vaccinating, so blood is not carried from one sheep to another.
Keep sheep well fed, with good minerals and regular deworming, so they are strong enough to recover if infected. Thin, wormy sheep suffer worse from any illness.
detail.impact: Bluetongue can be costly on a Kenyan sheep farm even when few animals die. Sick sheep stop eating for days to weeks and lose a lot of body condition, so they fetch much lower prices at market and take months to regain weight. Ewes may abort or give birth to weak or deformed lambs, which means a lost lambing season. Rams with fever can become temporarily infertile, which delays mating. Wool flocks suffer a wool break that ruins the fleece value for that clip. Lame sheep cannot walk to grazing and water, which is a serious problem in pastoral systems where flocks walk long distances. Deaths vary widely between outbreaks, breeds and serotypes. They can be significant in exotic or newly introduced sheep, while local flocks may lose few animals. There are also costs for vet visits, medicines, extra feed and labour for nursing. When bluetongue is confirmed in an area, some markets and buyers may restrict the movement or sale of animals, which adds to the losses.
detail.outlook: Many sheep, especially indigenous breeds and those with mild signs, recover fully over a few weeks with good nursing. Sheep with severe face swelling, extensive mouth sores, pneumonia or severe muscle damage have a guarded outlook. Some of these die or must be culled, and others stay thin and weak for a long time. Recovery is better when sick animals get early shade, easy access to water and soft feed, are housed away from midges, and receive vet-prescribed pain relief and treatment for complications. Recovery is worse in exotic breeds, very young or old animals, sheep already thin from poor feeding or worms, and sheep exposed to hot sun. Survivors are usually immune to that serotype, but they may still get sick from a different serotype in a later season. After recovery, expect wool breaks and hoof rings to appear, and some ewes may have reduced fertility for a while.

faqs.q: My sheep's tongue is not blue. Can it still be bluetongue?
faqs.a: Yes. Most sheep with bluetongue never get a blue tongue. The colour change happens only in some severe cases. Far more common signs are fever, drooling, a red sore mouth, a swollen face and lips, and lameness with red skin just above the hooves. If you see these in the rainy season, suspect bluetongue and call your vet.

faqs.q: Will bluetongue spread from my sick sheep to the healthy ones if they stay together?
faqs.a: Not by touch, sharing feed or breathing the same air. The virus moves from animal to animal mainly through the bites of midges. That is why keeping the whole flock under cover from dusk to dawn matters more than separating them. We still advise moving sick sheep into a quiet, shaded pen, so they can rest, drink and eat without competition and you can watch them closely.

faqs.q: My goats and cattle look healthy. Can they be part of the problem?
faqs.a: Yes. Cattle and goats are often infected without showing much illness. They can carry the virus in their blood for weeks, and midges pick it up from them and pass it to sheep. This is one reason bluetongue keeps coming back in mixed herds. Midge control around all your animals' housing helps protect the sheep.

faqs.q: Can I give my sick sheep an antibiotic from the agrovet to cure it?
faqs.a: No antibiotic cures bluetongue, because it is caused by a virus. Antibiotics only help when a vet finds a second, bacterial infection, such as pneumonia or badly infected sores. Using them without need wastes money, leaves drug residues in meat and milk, and helps bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. Let your vet examine the animals and decide.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat meat or drink milk from a sheep that had bluetongue?
faqs.a: Bluetongue does not infect people. Meat from an animal that has recovered and is passed fit by a meat inspector is not a risk from the virus itself. Do not slaughter very sick or feverish animals for food. If the sheep received any medicines, wait for the full withdrawal period your vet gives you before using its meat or milk.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine, and when should I use it?
faqs.a: Vaccines against bluetongue exist, but they must match the virus types in your area, and availability in Kenya can vary. Ask your County Veterinary Officer or private vet what is available locally. Vaccination is best done before the long or short rains, when midges are fewer. Your vet will advise how to handle pregnant ewes, as some vaccines should not be given in early pregnancy.

products.role: Sheep with sore mouths, fever and lameness often drink too little and become dehydrated. Offering RE-COVER oral rehydration solution in clean water can help maintain fluids, and it supports sheep coping with heat. Use it alongside shade, soft feed and the vet's treatment plan. It does not act against the bluetongue virus.

bluetongue.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a white-faced sheep in an East African boma, with a noticeably swollen muzzle, puffy lips and ears, and a string of saliva drooling from its mouth, standing in the shade on dry straw.
bluetongue.seoDescription: Bluetongue in sheep: spot swollen face, drooling, lameness and fever early, act before the vet arrives, and prevent midge-borne outbreaks in the rains.

card.headline: High fever with foul, bloody diarrhoea
card.look: A sheep, often one recently brought into the area, suddenly stops eating, stands dull with a hot body and a runny, sometimes blood-tinged nose. Within a day or two it passes watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea that may turn dark or bloody. Brown ear ticks are often seen on its ears.
card.action: Separate the sick sheep into shade with clean water, check the whole flock for ticks, and call your vet immediately.

aka: Ganjam virus disease (the same virus, as named in India)
detail.summary: Nairobi sheep disease is a viral disease of sheep and goats spread by the brown ear tick, the same tick that spreads East Coast fever in cattle. It causes a sudden high fever, nasal discharge, and foul diarrhoea that often becomes bloody, and it can kill many sheep in a flock within days. It strikes hardest when sheep that have never met the virus are moved into tick areas, or when ticks spread into new areas after heavy rains. There is no cure for the virus, so tick control and careful planning of animal movements are the farmer's best protection.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Nairobi sheep disease virus. This virus belongs to the same family as the virus that causes Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever in people. It is carried mainly by the brown ear tick (Rhipicephalus appendiculatus). When an infected tick feeds, it passes the virus into the sheep's blood. After a few days the virus multiplies in the blood and organs, causing a very high fever. It damages the lining of blood vessels and the gut, so the animal bleeds into the intestines and other tissues. This is why the diarrhoea becomes bloody and smells so bad. The animal loses a lot of fluid, becomes dehydrated (dried out) and weak, and the damaged gut lets bacteria into the body. Many sheep die within a few days of the fever starting. Pregnant ewes often abort. Sheep that survive usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity, meaning their body learns to fight the virus.
spread: The virus is spread by tick bites, mainly from the brown ear tick, which likes to sit inside and around the ears of sheep, goats and cattle.
Infected ticks can keep the virus through their life stages and can pass it to their eggs, so new generations of ticks on the pasture may already carry the virus.
Ticks can survive on pasture for a long time without feeding, so a field can stay dangerous even if no sheep have grazed there for many months.
Outbreaks often follow moving sheep from tick-free or low-tick areas into areas where the brown ear tick and the virus are common, because these sheep have no immunity.
Heavy or long rains increase tick numbers and can spread ticks into new areas, so outbreaks can appear in flocks that have lived safely in one place for years.
Sick sheep do not usually spread the disease directly to other sheep by contact, but ticks that fed on them can drop off and later feed on other animals.
Buying or bringing in tick-infested sheep, goats or cattle can introduce infected ticks onto your farm.
detail.atRisk: Sheep are more severely affected than goats, and cattle do not get sick, although cattle can carry the brown ear tick that spreads the virus. The animals at greatest risk are sheep that have never been exposed to the virus: improved breeds such as Dorper or Merino bought from tick-free farms, sheep brought from dry or highland areas into wetter tick zones, and flocks in areas where ticks have newly spread. Local sheep in areas where the disease has long been present are often immune because they were exposed when young, so the disease may go unnoticed there until new stock arrives. Adult sheep and pregnant ewes are badly affected; abortion is common. Risk rises during and after the long and short rains, when tick numbers peak. Free-range and pastoral flocks grazing tick-infested pasture, and flocks moved along trade or grazing routes, are most exposed, but zero-grazed sheep can still be infected if ticks come in on fodder, other animals or new stock.

early: A sudden high fever: the sheep feels hot to touch, especially inside the ears and between the legs, and a thermometer shows a temperature well above normal.
The sheep stops eating, stands apart from the flock with its head down, and is dull and unwilling to move.
Fast or laboured breathing even while resting.
A clear nasal discharge that soon becomes thick and may be streaked with blood.
Brown ear ticks found on the ears, head or neck, often in a flock recently moved or bought in.
Signs usually start a few days after the sheep arrive in a tick area or after a heavy tick challenge.
advanced: Watery, very foul-smelling diarrhoea that often turns dark, mucky or clearly bloody; the sheep may strain when passing dung.
Dirty, soiled hindquarters and tail from repeated diarrhoea.
Sunken eyes, dry gums and skin that stays tented when pinched, all signs of severe dehydration.
Red, swollen eyes and a bloody discharge from the nose; in some animals a swollen or reddened vulva.
Pregnant ewes aborting.
Extreme weakness, lying down and unable to rise, then death, often within a few days of the fever starting.
Several sheep in the same group falling sick and dying over a short time.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR also causes fever, nasal discharge and diarrhoea, but it usually affects goats more severely than sheep and causes sores and crusts on the gums, lips and tongue, foul breath, and pneumonia with coughing. It spreads by direct contact between animals, not by ticks. PPR is a notifiable disease, so if you see mouth sores, report to your County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater
lookalikes.howToTell: Heartwater is also tick-borne, but it is spread by the bont tick (Amblyomma), which has colourful patterned legs and body, not the plain brown ear tick. Heartwater commonly causes nervous signs such as high-stepping walking, chewing movements, circling, paddling the legs and convulsions. Bloody diarrhoea is less typical.

lookalikes.name: Rift Valley fever
lookalikes.howToTell: Rift Valley fever comes after heavy rains and flooding with large mosquito numbers. It causes waves of abortion and very high deaths in young lambs, and can make farm workers sick with fever. It is notifiable in Kenya and dangerous to people, so report any abortion storms to the County Veterinary Officer straight away and avoid handling aborted material bare-handed.

lookalikes.name: Salmonellosis and other bacterial gut infections
lookalikes.howToTell: These can also cause fever and bloody, smelly diarrhoea, but they are often linked to stress, dirty water, crowding or bad feed and are not tied to moving sheep into tick areas. Nasal discharge and breathing signs are less common. Only laboratory tests can reliably tell them apart.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will suspect Nairobi sheep disease from the history (sheep recently moved into a tick area, or heavy rains and ticks), the high fever, the bloody diarrhoea and the presence of brown ear ticks. The vet will examine sick animals, take their temperatures and check for ticks. Confirmation needs a laboratory. Blood samples from feverish animals, or tissues such as spleen and lymph nodes from a fresh carcass, can be tested to detect the virus (for example by PCR, a test that finds the virus's genetic material) or antibodies (proteins the body makes against the virus). In Kenya these tests can be arranged through the County Veterinary Officer and government veterinary laboratories. At post-mortem, the vet may find bleeding along the intestines, especially in the large intestine where it can look striped, a swollen spleen and swollen lymph nodes. Because Rift Valley fever and PPR can look similar, the vet may test for those too. To help, write down when the sheep arrived and where from, when signs started, how many are sick and how many have died, any abortions, what tick control you have used and when. Do not open dead animals yourself; keep a fresh carcass cool and covered for the vet if possible.
firstSteps: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer immediately, because sheep can die within days and the rest of the flock may already be infected.
Separate sick sheep into a quiet, shaded pen with good airflow and keep them away from healthy animals and from grazing pasture.
Give clean, fresh drinking water at all times and offer soft, palatable feed such as fresh grass or good hay, even if they eat little.
Check every sheep, goat and cattle animal on the farm for ticks, paying special attention to the ears, head and neck, and talk to your vet about tick control for the whole herd.
Stop moving sheep in or out of the farm and do not sell or buy animals until the vet has advised you.
Take the temperature of the rest of the flock daily if you have a thermometer, and separate any animal that has a fever or stops eating.
Wear gloves when handling sick animals, dung, aborted lambs or ticks, do not crush ticks with bare fingers, and wash your hands well with soap afterwards.
Record dates, numbers of sick and dead animals, signs seen and any treatments given, to help the vet and for future planning.
Do not slaughter sick sheep for meat; bury or dispose of carcasses safely as your vet advises, away from water sources and dogs.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the Nairobi sheep disease virus, so treatment is supportive, meaning it helps the animal's body survive while it fights the virus. Antibiotics do not cure the virus. A vet may give fluids by mouth or by drip to correct dehydration, an anti-inflammatory drug to bring down fever and pain, and, in some cases, an antibiotic to control bacteria that invade the damaged gut. Antibiotics should only be used when the vet judges they are needed, because careless use leads to antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working for animals and people. The vet will also plan urgent tick control for all animals on the farm, using acaricides (tick-killing chemicals) such as amitraz or synthetic pyrethroids by dipping, spraying or pour-on, with careful attention to the ears. All medicines and acaricides have milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time you must wait before milk or meat can be used for food, and these must be followed. Treatment must be prescribed by a vet; doses depend on the product and the animal. Even with good care, many severely affected sheep still die, especially those already weak, dehydrated or lying down when treatment starts.
prevention: Plan movements carefully: avoid moving sheep from tick-free or low-tick areas into brown ear tick areas, and if you must, discuss with your vet first.
Before moving sheep into a tick area, and for several weeks after arrival, keep them under strict tick control so infected ticks cannot feed on them.
Use a regular tick control programme for sheep, goats and cattle together, since all can carry the brown ear tick; treat more often during the long and short rains when ticks peak.
When using sprays or dips, make sure the acaricide reaches inside and around the ears, where brown ear ticks gather, and follow the label for mixing, interval and withdrawal periods.
Rotate acaricide types only as advised by your vet or agrovet, because ticks can become resistant if products are misused.
Quarantine newly bought animals for at least two to three weeks, check them for ticks and treat them before they join your flock.
Keep grass short around sheds and night pens, and avoid grazing new or valuable sheep on heavily tick-infested pasture, especially bushy areas.
There is no widely available commercial vaccine for Nairobi sheep disease in Kenya; ask your County Veterinary Officer about any current options.
Keep sheep well fed, with clean water, minerals and good parasite control, so they are stronger if they are infected.
detail.impact: Nairobi sheep disease can wipe out a large part of a flock in a short time. Farmers who invest in improved breeding rams or ewes, such as Dorper, from tick-free areas can lose that whole investment within days of arrival. Pregnant ewes abort, so the next lamb crop is lost. Surviving sheep lose weight and condition and take weeks to recover, delaying sales. Costs add up from vet visits, supportive treatment, lab tests and more frequent tick control. The disease also discourages farmers from improving their flocks and limits the safe movement of sheep between regions for trade and breeding.
detail.humanHealth: Nairobi sheep disease virus has only rarely been reported to infect people, mostly laboratory workers, and the illness has usually been a mild fever. However, it is closely related to the virus that causes Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, and ticks on sheep can carry other diseases that affect people. Wear gloves when handling sick animals, blood, dung, aborted lambs and carcasses, and do not crush ticks with bare hands. Do not eat meat from sheep that were sick or died of the disease. If you treat animals, respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods for all drugs and acaricides so residues do not end up in food. If anyone handling sick sheep develops a fever, they should see a health worker and mention the animal contact.
detail.outlook: The outlook for sheep that become clearly sick is poor, and many die within a few days, especially those that have never been exposed before. Animals with milder illness, or that get early supportive care with fluids and good nursing, have a better chance. Sheep that recover usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity and are unlikely to get sick again. The outlook for the rest of the flock depends heavily on how fast tick control is put in place to stop more infected ticks from feeding. Local sheep in long-affected areas often have immunity and rarely show disease.

faqs.q: My local sheep have lived here for years without problems. Why did only the new rams I bought fall sick?
faqs.a: Local sheep in an area where the virus is common are usually exposed when young, survive and become immune. New sheep from a tick-free or low-tick area have no immunity, so when infected brown ear ticks bite them they become very sick. This is why the disease is so often seen in newly bought or moved sheep. Keep new stock under strict tick control and talk to your vet before bringing sheep in from other areas.

faqs.q: Can my goats and cattle get Nairobi sheep disease?
faqs.a: Goats can get it, but they are usually less severely affected than sheep. Cattle do not become sick, but they often carry brown ear ticks, which can then move to sheep. That is why tick control should cover all your animals, not just the sheep. Good tick control also protects your cattle from East Coast fever, which is spread by the same tick.

faqs.q: Can a sick sheep spread the disease to the rest of my flock just by being close?
faqs.a: The disease does not spread easily from sheep to sheep by contact. It needs ticks to carry it. But ticks that feed on a sick sheep can drop off and later bite other animals, so isolating the sick sheep and controlling ticks across the whole farm is still important.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine I can buy at the agrovet?
faqs.a: Vaccines have been developed and tested in the past, but there is no widely available commercial vaccine for Nairobi sheep disease in Kenya at present. Prevention depends on tick control and careful planning of animal movements. Ask your County Veterinary Officer if any vaccine becomes available in your area.

faqs.q: Can I slaughter a sick sheep and eat the meat to avoid a total loss?
faqs.a: No. Meat from a sick, feverish animal is unsafe and poor quality, and handling the blood and organs of a sick animal carries a risk to you. If the sheep has been treated, drug residues may also be in the meat. Let your vet confirm the cause and advise on safe disposal.

faqs.q: If a sheep recovers, can it get the disease again?
faqs.a: Sheep that survive usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity and are unlikely to become sick from this virus again. They may take several weeks to regain weight and condition. Keep up good feeding, clean water and tick control while they recover.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help replace water and salts lost through diarrhoea and fever, used as part of supportive nursing alongside your vet's treatment and tick control. It does not act against the virus; ask your vet whether and how to use it for each sick sheep.
