card.headline: Pale eyelids and swollen bottle jaw
card.look: The inside of the lower eyelid is pale pink or white instead of healthy red, and there may be a soft, cool swelling under the jaw. The sheep is weak, lags behind the flock and may suddenly die after the rains.
card.action: Check the eyelid colour of every sheep, gently separate pale or weak ones without chasing them, and call your vet or animal health officer the same day.

detail.summary: Haemonchosis is disease caused by the barber's pole worm, Haemonchus contortus, a blood-sucking worm that lives in the fourth stomach of sheep and goats. Large numbers of worms drain so much blood that sheep become severely anaemic (short of blood), weak and swollen under the jaw, and many die suddenly. In Kenya and across East Africa it is one of the most important killers of sheep, especially in the weeks after the long and short rains. Early detection using eyelid colour checks (the FAMACHA method) and correct, targeted deworming saves lives and slows the spread of dewormer resistance.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Haemonchus contortus, a roundworm about two to three centimetres long that attaches to the lining of the abomasum, the true or fourth stomach. It pierces the stomach wall with a small tooth-like lancet and sucks blood. The female worm looks like a red and white twisted stripe, like an old barber's pole, because her blood-filled gut twists around her white egg tubes. Each worm takes only a little blood, but a sheep can carry thousands of worms, so the total blood loss can be very large and very fast. As blood drains away the sheep becomes anaemic, meaning it has too few red blood cells to carry oxygen, so it tires easily and breathes fast. The sheep also loses blood protein. When protein in the blood falls low, fluid leaks out of the blood vessels and collects under the jaw, causing the soft swelling called bottle jaw. Unlike many other worms, barber's pole worm does not usually cause diarrhoea, so a sheep can look clean at the back end while it is quietly bleeding to death inside. Female worms lay thousands of eggs every day, which pass out in the dung and contaminate the pasture very quickly.
spread: Infected sheep and goats pass worm eggs in their dung onto pasture, around water points and in bomas, and each female worm can lay thousands of eggs a day.
In warm, wet weather the eggs hatch and develop into infective larvae within about a week, which is why outbreaks follow the long and short rains.
The infective larvae climb up wet grass blades in dew, mist and after rain, and sheep swallow them while grazing, especially when grazing short grass close to the ground.
Swallowed larvae become egg-laying adults in roughly three weeks, so a heavily contaminated pasture can produce a crisis within a month of the rains starting.
During the dry season some larvae rest inside the sheep's stomach wall in a sleeping stage, then wake up together when conditions improve, causing sudden heavy infections.
Ewes around lambing and during early milking have lower immunity and shed many more eggs, which contaminates pasture just as young lambs start grazing.
Buying sheep or goats from markets without quarantine and deworming brings in new worms, including worms already resistant to common dewormers.
Shared communal grazing, overstocked paddocks and grazing the same small plot year-round build up large numbers of larvae on the grass.
detail.atRisk: All sheep can be affected, but lambs and weaners from weaning to about one year old are most at risk because they have not yet built immunity. Ewes in late pregnancy and early lactation are also highly vulnerable because their immunity drops around lambing. Thin, poorly fed sheep, and sheep with other diseases, suffer worse because they cannot replace lost blood and protein. Risk is highest during and soon after the long rains (around March to June) and short rains (around October to December), and in warm, humid areas such as the coast, Lake Victoria basin and highland areas with good rainfall. Free-range and communal grazing systems, and small overstocked paddocks grazed continuously, carry the highest risk. Zero-grazed sheep are at lower risk but can still be infected if cut grass is harvested close to the ground from wet, contaminated areas. Some breeds handle worms better than others: the indigenous Red Maasai sheep is well known for its resistance to Haemonchus, while Dorper, Merino and many exotic and crossbred sheep tend to be more susceptible. Goats grazing with sheep share the same worm and suffer just as badly.

early: The inside of the lower eyelid is pale pink instead of bright red when you gently pull it down.
The gums and inside of the lips look paler than usual.
The sheep tires quickly, lags behind the flock when walking to grazing or water, and may lie down more often.
Slower growth and weight gain in lambs, or slight loss of body condition in adults, even though feed looks enough.
The wool or hair may look dull, dry and rough, and the fleece may break or shed easily.
Breathing becomes faster after a short walk or after being handled.
Dung usually stays normal pellets, so the absence of diarrhoea does not rule out this worm.
advanced: The eyelids, gums and skin inside the ears are very pale, almost white.
A soft, cool, fluid-filled swelling appears under the jaw (bottle jaw), often bigger in the evening after grazing with the head down and smaller in the morning.
Severe weakness, staggering, reluctance to stand, or collapse when driven or handled.
Rapid, laboured breathing and a fast heartbeat even at rest.
Marked weight loss and a thin, bony back and hips.
In very heavy infections, especially in lambs after the rains, sheep may die suddenly with few warning signs, sometimes several in a short period.
Ewes may abort, produce weak lambs or have little milk.

lookalikes.name: Liver fluke (fasciolosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Liver fluke also causes pale eyelids, bottle jaw and weight loss, so the two are easily confused. Fluke is more common where sheep graze swampy areas, dams, irrigation channels or river banks where water snails live, and it often builds up more slowly. A vet can tell them apart with dung tests (fluke eggs need a different test) or at post-mortem, where fluke shows as flat leaf-shaped worms in a damaged liver rather than small red worms in the stomach. Both can occur together.

lookalikes.name: Scour worms (Trichostrongylus and other gut worms)
lookalikes.howToTell: These worms damage the gut lining and mainly cause diarrhoea, a dirty back end and weight loss. Sheep may be thin and weak but the eyelids usually stay fairly red. Barber's pole worm typically causes pale eyelids without diarrhoea. Mixed infections are common, so a dung test helps.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomosis (nagana) and tick-borne anaemia
lookalikes.howToTell: Trypanosomosis, spread by tsetse flies, and tick-borne blood parasites such as anaplasmosis also cause pale eyelids and weakness. These are more likely in tsetse or heavily tick-infested areas and often come with fever, swollen lymph nodes, or yellowish eyelids. A vet confirms them with a blood smear rather than a dung test.

lookalikes.name: Poor nutrition or mineral deficiency (such as cobalt deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: Underfed sheep or those lacking minerals such as cobalt and copper become thin, weak and may be mildly pale, but this develops slowly across the whole flock and does not follow the rains. Bottle jaw and sudden deaths are much less typical. Pale sheep that improve quickly after effective deworming point strongly to worms.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer usually starts by checking eyelid colour, gums, body condition and the area under the jaw, and by asking about recent rains, grazing and the last deworming date and product. Many use the FAMACHA chart, a card developed in South Africa that compares eyelid colour to five shades from red (category 1, healthy) to white (category 5, severely anaemic). A blood sample can measure the packed cell volume (PCV), which shows exactly how anaemic the sheep is. Dung samples are examined under a microscope to count worm eggs per gram (a faecal egg count, often by the McMaster method), and a larval culture can confirm that the eggs are Haemonchus rather than other worms. If a sheep dies, a post-mortem is very useful: the carcass looks pale, the blood is watery, and many small red and white worms are seen moving in the stomach contents. To check whether your dewormer still works, the vet may do a faecal egg count reduction test, comparing egg counts before and about ten to fourteen days after treatment. You can help by recording which sheep are pale and when, the dewormer brand, batch and date last used, and how you calculated the dose. Collect fresh dung pellets straight from the rectum or immediately after passing into a clean labelled bag, keep it cool, and get it to the lab within a day. If a sheep dies, keep the body cool and covered and call the vet quickly so a post-mortem can be done.
firstSteps: Check the eyelid colour of every sheep and goat in the flock, not just the sick ones, and write down which animals look pale, very pale or have bottle jaw.
Move weak and very pale sheep slowly and calmly into a shaded, quiet pen near the homestead; do not chase, drive hard or wrestle them, because severely anaemic sheep can collapse and die from stress.
Give clean, fresh water and good quality feed such as fresh-cut grass harvested higher up the stem, hay, and some protein-rich forage such as lucerne, desmodium or calliandra if available.
Keep the sick sheep off the contaminated grazing area for now, and avoid grazing the rest of the flock on wet, short grass early in the morning while dew is still on it.
Call your vet, animal health officer or a trusted agrovet with animal health staff the same day, and tell them the eyelid scores, how many animals are affected and which dewormer you last used.

Do not give any dewormer or injection until you have spoken to a vet, because many worms in Kenya are already resistant to common dewormers and a wrong choice can waste money and time while the sheep keeps bleeding.
If a sheep dies, keep the carcass cool and covered away from dogs, and ask the vet to do a post-mortem so the cause can be confirmed for the rest of the flock.
Wash your hands after handling sheep and dung, and keep a simple notebook of dates, animals and treatments to help plan future worm control.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment is with an anthelmintic (dewormer) chosen and prescribed by the vet. The main drug groups that act against barber's pole worm include benzimidazoles (for example albendazole and fenbendazole), imidazothiazoles (levamisole), macrocyclic lactones (for example ivermectin, doramectin and moxidectin), salicylanilides such as closantel, which is narrow-spectrum and mainly targets blood-sucking worms and liver fluke, and newer groups such as monepantel where available. Resistance of Haemonchus to benzimidazoles, levamisole and ivermectin has been reported in Kenya and the region, so the vet will choose a product based on local experience, your farm history and, ideally, a faecal egg count reduction test. Sometimes a combination of drug groups is advised. The dose must be based on accurate body weight: guessing weight is a leading cause of under-dosing, which fails to kill worms and speeds up resistance. The vet may recommend weighing sheep or using a weigh band, and will show you how to give an oral drench correctly over the back of the tongue. Often the vet will recommend treating only the pale animals (FAMACHA categories 4 and 5, and sometimes 3) rather than the whole flock, so that some worms that have never met the drug survive on the pasture; this is called keeping refugia and helps the drug keep working longer. Very weak sheep may also need supportive care such as iron or vitamin B12 injections, good feeding with protein, rest and shelter, and in rare valuable cases a blood transfusion. Antibiotics do not kill worms and are not a treatment for haemonchosis. After effective treatment the worms die within days, but rebuilding lost blood takes several weeks, so sheep stay weak for a while and must be handled gently. Every dewormer has a meat withdrawal period, and many have a milk withdrawal period, during which the animal must not be slaughtered or its milk used; some, such as closantel and long-acting products, have long withdrawal times. Follow the vet's and label's instructions exactly and record the date.
prevention: Check eyelid colour with a FAMACHA chart every one to two weeks during and after the rains, and monthly in the dry season, and treat only the sheep that are pale; ask your County livestock or veterinary office about FAMACHA training, as charts should be used by trained people.
Use the Five Point Check when you handle sheep: eyes for paleness, jaw for swelling, back for body condition, tail area for diarrhoea, and nose for discharge, so you catch worm problems early.
Work with your vet to use faecal egg counts before and after deworming at least once a year, to find out which dewormers still work on your farm.

Weigh sheep or use a weigh band before deworming, dose for the correct weight as instructed, use a calibrated drench gun, and never mix your own diluted products or buy unlabelled dewormers of doubtful quality.
Avoid deworming the whole flock too often; frequent blanket treatment is the fastest way to create resistant worms that no dewormer can kill.

Rotate grazing so paddocks rest for several weeks before sheep return, graze sheep after cattle or with cattle, which do not carry this worm, and avoid overgrazing to the ground, because most larvae live in the bottom few centimetres of grass.

In zero-grazing, cut fodder higher up the stem, avoid cutting from wet, dung-contaminated areas around homesteads and water points, feed in raised troughs or racks off the floor, and remove dung regularly.
Quarantine all newly bought sheep and goats for at least two to three weeks, have the vet advise on an effective quarantine drench, and keep them off clean pasture until their dung is checked.
Feed well, especially ewes in late pregnancy and lactation and weaned lambs, because well-fed sheep with enough protein and minerals resist worms better and recover lost blood faster.

Choose or cross with worm-tolerant breeds such as the Red Maasai where suitable, and cull sheep that repeatedly become pale despite good management, while keeping those that rarely need treatment as breeding stock.
detail.impact: Barber's pole worm is one of the biggest causes of sheep losses on Kenyan smallholder and pastoral farms. Deaths of lambs, weaners and ewes after the rains can wipe out a season's profit and breeding stock in a few weeks. Even sheep that survive grow slowly, take longer to reach market weight, fetch lower prices at the market because they look thin and pale, and produce poorer wool and less milk for their lambs. Ewes may abort or produce weak lambs, cutting the next generation. Farmers spend money on repeated dewormers, and when those dewormers no longer work because of resistance, the money is wasted and the flock remains at risk. Labour, vet fees and replacement stock add further cost. Good worm control, on the other hand, is one of the cheapest and most effective ways to improve sheep productivity.
detail.humanHealth: Barber's pole worm does not infect people, so handling infected sheep or eating properly cooked meat from them does not give you this worm. The main human health concern is drug residues: meat and milk from sheep treated with dewormers must not be used until the withdrawal period on the label or advised by the vet has passed. Some dewormers, such as closantel and long-acting injections, have long withdrawal times. Always record treatment dates, keep dewormers locked away from children, and wash your hands after drenching and handling dung.
detail.outlook: Outlook depends mainly on how pale the sheep is when treatment starts and whether the dewormer used still works on your farm. Sheep with mild to moderate paleness that receive an effective dewormer, rest and good feed usually recover well over several weeks as they rebuild blood. Sheep with white eyelids, large bottle jaw, collapse or very rapid breathing are in danger and may die even with treatment, especially if stressed by handling or long walks. Lambs and thin ewes are more fragile. If the worms on your farm are resistant, sheep may not improve after deworming, which is why a follow-up eyelid check and egg count are important. Without changes to grazing and worm management the problem usually returns with the next rains, but farms that use FAMACHA, targeted treatment, rested pasture and good nutrition can greatly reduce losses.

faqs.q: I dewormed my sheep, but they are still pale and some died after the rains. Why?
faqs.a: There are several common reasons. The worms on your farm may be resistant to the dewormer you used, which is now widespread in Kenya for some of the older drug groups. The dose may have been too low because the weight was guessed, the product may have been of poor quality or expired, or the drench may have spilled. Sheep also go straight back onto heavily contaminated pasture after deworming and pick up new larvae. Finally, even after the worms die, a sheep needs several weeks to rebuild its blood, so it can stay weak for a while. Ask your vet for a faecal egg count before and after treatment to find out whether your dewormer is still working.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm my sheep?
faqs.a: There is no single calendar that suits every farm, and deworming the whole flock every month is one of the main causes of resistance. A better approach is to check eyelid colour every one to two weeks in the rainy season and monthly in the dry season, and to treat only sheep that are pale, plus any with bottle jaw or poor condition. Your vet may also advise strategic treatment of high-risk groups such as weaners and ewes near lambing, timed around the rains. Plan this with your vet based on your area, grazing system and egg count results.

faqs.q: Can I use the same dewormer for my sheep, goats and cattle?
faqs.a: Many dewormers are labelled for more than one species, but the correct dose, product and withdrawal time differ between species. Goats, for example, break down some dewormers faster than sheep, so a sheep dose may be too low for a goat. Sheep and goats share the same barber's pole worm, so worms resistant in goats will also be resistant in sheep grazing with them. Always read the label and ask your vet which product and dose to use for each species.

faqs.q: Bottle jaw means my sheep has liver fluke, doesn't it?
faqs.a: Not always. Bottle jaw happens whenever a sheep loses too much blood protein, and both barber's pole worm and liver fluke can cause it. Barber's pole worm is often the more common cause after the rains in many parts of Kenya, while fluke is more likely where sheep graze swampy areas or around dams. Many dewormers kill only one of these, so ask your vet to test the dung for both before choosing a product.

faqs.q: Do herbal or traditional dewormers work against barber's pole worm?
faqs.a: Some plants and tanniferous forages, meaning forages rich in natural compounds called tannins, have been studied for their effect on worms and may help reduce worm burdens as part of good management. However, results vary widely and most traditional remedies have not been proven to reliably kill Haemonchus in a severely sick sheep. A very pale sheep with bottle jaw needs a proven, effective dewormer prescribed by a vet straight away. Good nutrition, rested pasture and resistant breeds are the most reliable natural ways to reduce the problem over time.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat the meat of a sheep that had worms?
faqs.a: The barber's pole worm does not infect people, so meat from a sheep that had this worm is not a direct risk once properly inspected and cooked. However, very anaemic sheep produce poor quality, watery meat, and if the sheep was recently dewormed, you must wait until the withdrawal period has passed before slaughter. Never slaughter a sick sheep for sale without veterinary or meat inspection, and do not sell meat or milk from animals still within a dewormer withdrawal period.

card.headline: Soft swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw)
card.look: Thin, weak sheep with pale eyelids and gums and a soft, watery swelling under the jaw, often in flocks that graze swampy areas, dam edges or riverbanks. In heavy outbreaks, sheep that looked fine may be found dead with no warning.
card.action: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer to confirm fluke and prescribe the right flukicide, and move the flock off wet, snail-infested grazing straight away.

detail.summary: Liver fluke is a disease caused by flat, leaf-shaped worms called flukes that live in the liver and bile ducts of sheep. Sheep pick it up by eating grass from wet ground where tiny water snails live. A heavy dose of young flukes at once can tear up the liver and kill sheep suddenly, while a slower, long-term infection causes anaemia, bottle jaw and wasting. Sheep are more easily harmed by fluke than cattle, so it is a major cause of losses wherever sheep graze near swamps, dams and irrigated land.
detail.cause: Liver fluke is caused by flatworms of the genus Fasciola. In most of Kenya and East Africa the main species is Fasciola gigantica, the giant liver fluke. Fasciola hepatica, the common liver fluke, is also found, mainly in cooler, wetter highland areas. The fluke cannot complete its life without a small freshwater snail, called the intermediate host. Fluke eggs pass out in sheep dung. In water they hatch into tiny swimming larvae that enter snails and multiply many times inside them. Weeks later, large numbers of new larvae leave the snail, swim onto grass and water plants, and form hard cysts, the infective stage. When a sheep eats this grass, the young flukes break out in the gut, bore through the gut wall and travel into the liver. For several weeks they tunnel through the liver tissue, feeding and causing bleeding and damage. This is what causes acute disease and sudden death when many flukes arrive at once. The survivors settle in the bile ducts, the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the gut. There the adult flukes suck blood, thicken and block the ducts, and lay eggs for months or even years. The steady blood loss causes anaemia, and the damaged liver cannot make enough protein. Low blood protein lets fluid leak out under the skin, which is why bottle jaw appears. Damaged liver tissue can also allow a bacterium called Clostridium novyi to grow, causing black disease, another cause of sudden death.
spread: Sheep become infected by eating grass, reeds or water plants carrying fluke cysts, mainly from swamp edges, river banks, dam and water-pan margins, flooded fields and leaking irrigation channels.
Water snails are essential for spread, so any place where snails live, such as slow-moving or standing water, muddy hoof-marked ground and wet patches around taps or troughs, is a risk.
Cut-and-carry grass and napier harvested from swampy ground can bring fluke cysts into a zero-grazing unit, so even housed sheep can be infected.
Infected sheep, goats, cattle and wild animals drop fluke eggs in dung near water, which keeps the cycle going on shared grazing and watering points.
Risk rises during and after the long and short rains, when snails multiply, and in the dry season when animals crowd around the last remaining wet areas to graze and drink.
Buying sheep from fluke areas or moving them through wet grazing on the way to market can bring fluke onto a farm that was previously clean, if suitable snail habitat exists there.
Fluke does not pass directly from sheep to sheep; it always needs the snail stage in between.
detail.atRisk: All sheep of any breed or age can be infected, and sheep do not build up strong immunity, so adults remain at risk year after year. Young lambs grazing contaminated pasture for the first time and pregnant or nursing ewes often suffer most. Flocks in high-rainfall highland areas, around the Lake Victoria basin, near swamps, in irrigation schemes and along rivers are at highest risk, as are pastoral flocks that gather at dams and water pans during the dry season. Zero-grazed sheep fed on grass cut from wet valley bottoms are also at risk. Acute disease usually appears some weeks after a period when sheep have eaten large numbers of cysts, often towards the end of the rains or early in the dry season, while chronic disease is seen for months afterwards.

early: Sheep gradually lose weight or fail to gain, even though feed seems adequate.
The flock looks dull, slower on walks and lags behind others.
Pale pink or white eyelids and gums instead of a healthy red, a sign of anaemia (lack of red blood).
Rough, dry or brittle wool or hair coat and reduced wool growth.
Ewes produce less milk and lambs grow poorly.
In acute cases, sheep may be weak, reluctant to move and stand hunched, and may show pain when the right side of the belly is pressed.
advanced: Soft, cold, watery swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw), often bigger in the evening after grazing with the head down.
Severe weakness, very white gums and eyelids, and fast breathing after slight effort.
Marked wasting, with the backbone and hip bones sticking out.
Swollen, fluid-filled belly in some sheep.
Ewes may abort, fail to get pregnant, or give birth to weak lambs.
Sudden deaths, sometimes several in a few days, in sheep that looked normal shortly before, especially in acute outbreaks or with black disease.

lookalikes.name: Barber's pole worm (haemonchosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Also causes pale eyelids, bottle jaw and sudden deaths, and is very common in Kenya. It often hits lambs and young sheep hard during the rains, and does not require swampy grazing. Only a lab can tell them apart reliably: a normal worm egg test (flotation) finds Haemonchus eggs, while fluke eggs need a special sedimentation test. Sheep can have both at once.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia or other clostridial disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Causes sudden death, often in well-fed, fast-growing lambs after a change to rich feed, not in thin, pale sheep. A vet's post-mortem shows a liver tunnelled with fluke tracks in acute fluke, versus other changes in enterotoxaemia.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomosis (nagana)
lookalikes.howToTell: Also causes anaemia and wasting, but occurs in tsetse fly areas and often comes with fever, swollen lymph nodes and watery eyes. A blood smear examined by a vet or lab can show trypanosomes.

lookalikes.name: Johne's disease, poor teeth or underfeeding
lookalikes.howToTell: These cause wasting, but sheep usually do not have the very pale gums and bottle jaw typical of fluke. Check teeth and feed supply, and ask the vet for faecal and blood tests if wasting continues.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock history, grazing near water, the season, and signs such as pale membranes, bottle jaw and wasting. The most common test is a faecal sedimentation test, which looks for fluke eggs in fresh dung; ordinary worm egg counts often miss them. Eggs only appear once flukes are adults, so in acute disease the dung test may be negative even when sheep are dying. Labs may also offer a coproantigen test, which detects fluke material in dung earlier, and blood tests showing anaemia, low blood protein and raised liver enzymes. Post-mortem examination is often the quickest and surest answer: the vet sees a swollen, bleeding liver with tunnels from young flukes, or thick, hard bile ducts full of adult flukes. Slaughterhouse reports of condemned livers are also useful clues. To help, the farmer can collect fresh dung samples from several sheep in clean labelled bags kept cool, keep any recently dead sheep in a shaded, covered place for the vet, and note where the flock grazes and drinks, when signs started, recent deaths and all dewormers used with dates.
firstSteps: Call your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a trusted animal health assistant early, especially if sheep are dying suddenly or several have bottle jaw.
Move the flock off swampy ground, dam edges and riverbanks immediately, and fence off wet patches where possible.
Stop feeding grass cut from wet valley bottoms or swamp edges; use grass from drier ground or well-dried hay instead.
Separate weak, pale or swollen-jawed sheep into a quiet, shaded pen close to clean water and good feed.
Handle anaemic sheep gently and avoid chasing, long walks or dipping, because very weak sheep can collapse and die from stress.
Provide clean drinking water from troughs or tanks rather than letting sheep drink from ponds or streams.
Give the best feed you have, including good hay, legumes or some concentrate, to support sheep that are losing condition.
Write down which sheep are affected, deaths, where the flock grazed in the last two to three months, and every dewormer given with dates, and keep dung samples or dead sheep ready for the vet.
detail.vetTreatment: Liver fluke is treated with drugs called flukicides, which must be chosen and prescribed by a vet. This matters because many common dewormers, including ivermectin and levamisole, do not kill fluke at all. Commonly used flukicides include triclabendazole, closantel, nitroxynil, oxyclozanide and albendazole. They differ greatly in which fluke stages they kill: triclabendazole is the main product that kills the very young migrating flukes that cause acute disease, while others such as oxyclozanide and albendazole act mainly on adult flukes. The vet will pick a product based on whether disease is acute or chronic, the time of year, and whether a combined worm and fluke product makes sense. A repeat treatment is often needed some weeks later to kill flukes that were too young the first time. Fluke resistance to triclabendazole has been reported in several countries, so the vet may check whether treatment worked with a follow-up dung test. Antibiotics do not kill flukes. Severely affected sheep also need rest, good feed and protein to rebuild blood and liver, and the vet may advise clostridial vaccination because of black disease. Flukicides have meat withdrawal periods, some of them long, and many are not permitted at all in sheep producing milk for people, so follow the label and the vet's advice before selling or slaughtering sheep or using milk. Expect chronic cases to improve slowly over weeks, while some very weak sheep may still die after treatment because of the damage already done.
prevention: Work with your vet or County Veterinary Officer to plan strategic fluke treatments timed to local rains and seasons, usually after the main transmission period, rather than treating at random.
Fence off or avoid grazing swamps, dam and water-pan edges, riverbanks and leaking irrigation areas, especially during and after the rains.
Provide clean water in troughs or tanks away from snail habitat, and repair leaking pipes, taps and troughs that create muddy, wet patches.
Cut grass for zero-grazing from dry, upland ground, not from wet valley bottoms, or let cut grass dry well before feeding; thoroughly dried hay carries much lower risk than fresh grass.
Drain small wet areas where practical, but avoid using chemicals to kill snails in natural water bodies because they harm fish, livestock and the environment.
Treat newly bought sheep with a suitable flukicide on the vet's advice and keep them away from wet grazing until treated.
Vaccinate sheep against clostridial diseases, including black disease, as part of routine flock health, following your vet's advice.
Check pale eyelids and body condition regularly, send dung samples for fluke testing at least once or twice a year, and ask for slaughterhouse feedback on livers.
Remember that cattle and goats sharing the grazing also carry fluke, so plan control for all grazing animals together.
detail.impact: Liver fluke costs Kenyan sheep farmers money quietly and steadily. Acute outbreaks can kill several sheep within days, a heavy loss for a smallholder with a small flock. Chronic fluke is more common and harder to notice: sheep grow slowly, take longer to reach market weight, give less milk to lambs, produce less and poorer wool, and ewes may fail to conceive, abort or raise weak lambs. Thin, anaemic sheep fetch low prices at market. Infected livers are condemned at slaughter, so butchers and slaughterhouses lose value. Farmers also spend money on repeated treatments, sometimes on the wrong dewormers that do not kill fluke, which wastes money and speeds up worm resistance. Because fluke also infects cattle and goats on shared grazing, the total loss to a mixed farm or pastoral community can be large.
detail.humanHealth: People can get liver fluke (human fascioliasis), but not directly from touching sheep or from eating well-cooked liver or meat. People are infected the same way as sheep: by eating raw water plants, such as watercress or other greens from swamps and streams, or by drinking untreated water carrying fluke cysts. Human cases in Kenya are uncommon, but the risk is real near infected grazing. Wash and cook vegetables from wet areas, drink boiled or treated water, and do not eat livers that a meat inspector has condemned. Flukicide drugs leave residues in meat and milk, so always respect withdrawal periods before slaughtering treated sheep or using their milk.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how heavy the infection is and how early it is treated. Sheep with mild to moderate chronic fluke usually recover well after the right flukicide, good feeding and removal from wet grazing, although regaining weight and wool takes weeks to months. Sheep with severe anaemia, marked bottle jaw and wasting have a poorer chance, and some die even after treatment because the liver is badly scarred. In acute outbreaks, some sheep may already be beyond help, but prompt treatment with a product that kills young flukes and moving the flock off contaminated pasture can stop further deaths. Sheep do not become immune, so without prevention the problem will return each wet season.

faqs.q: I deworm my sheep regularly. Why do they still have liver fluke?
faqs.a: Many common dewormers, such as ivermectin and levamisole, do not kill fluke at all. Others kill only adult flukes and miss the young ones in the liver. Ask your vet or agrovet to check that the product you use is labelled for liver fluke in sheep, and time treatment to your local fluke season.

faqs.q: My sheep never graze near the swamp. How can they have fluke?
faqs.a: Fluke cysts can come in on cut grass or napier harvested from wet ground, from small wet patches around leaking taps or troughs, or from drinking at streams on the way to grazing. Bought-in sheep can also arrive already infected. Look carefully for any wet spots or feed sources linked to water.

faqs.q: Can I eat the liver of a sheep that had fluke?
faqs.a: A liver full of flukes is usually condemned by meat inspectors because it is damaged and unfit to eat. Well-cooked meat and liver do not give people fluke, because people catch it from raw water plants and dirty water. Still, do not eat condemned livers, and respect drug withdrawal periods after treatment.

faqs.q: How often should I treat for liver fluke?
faqs.a: It depends on your area, rainfall and how much wet grazing your sheep use. In high-risk areas vets often advise two or more strategic treatments a year, timed after the rains when infection has been picked up. Your vet or County Veterinary Officer can help you set a plan that fits local seasons.

faqs.q: Do goats and cattle on my farm also need treatment?
faqs.a: Yes, cattle, goats and some wild animals carry the same fluke and drop eggs that keep snails infected. If only the sheep are treated, the pasture stays contaminated. Plan fluke control for all grazing animals that share land and water.

faqs.q: Should I poison the snails in the swamp?
faqs.a: Chemicals that kill snails also harm fish, other water life and sometimes livestock and people, so they are not generally recommended for natural water. Fencing off wet areas, providing trough water, careful grass cutting and well-timed treatment are safer and more practical.

products.role: Can be given alongside the vet-prescribed flukicide and better feeding to support liver function and digestion while fluke-damaged sheep recover; it does not kill flukes or replace treatment and grazing management.

card.headline: Limping sheep grazing on their knees
card.look: One or more sheep limp, hold up a foot or graze kneeling down. Between the toes the skin is moist and grey, the hoof horn is lifting away, and there is a strong, rotten, cheesy smell you cannot mistake.
card.action: Catch and check every lame sheep's feet today, separate the affected ones onto dry ground, and call your vet to confirm foot rot and plan treatment.

aka: Kuoza kwato (Swahili description: rotting of the hoof)
detail.summary: Foot rot is a contagious bacterial infection of the sheep's foot. It starts as inflammation of the skin between the toes and can spread under the hoof horn until the horn separates from the foot underneath. It is very painful, so affected sheep limp, graze on their knees, lose weight and produce less. Once it is in a flock it spreads quickly in wet, warm weather and is hard to get rid of unless the whole flock is managed together.
detail.cause: The main cause is a bacterium called Dichelobacter nodosus. It works together with another bacterium, Fusobacterium necrophorum, which lives naturally in manure and soil. Both are anaerobic, which means they thrive where there is little oxygen, such as inside damp, damaged skin. When the skin between the claws stays wet for a long time it softens and gets small injuries. Fusobacterium gets in first and causes redness and moisture, a stage often called scald. If D. nodosus is present, it then invades. It produces enzymes (natural chemicals) that break down the soft tissue joining the hoof horn to the sensitive foot inside. The horn starts lifting from the heel and sole, and in severe cases from the wall of the hoof as well. This is called 'underrunning'. The dead tissue underneath produces the typical foul smell. Some strains of D. nodosus are mild (benign) and cause mostly scald, while others are virulent and cause severe underrunning. You cannot tell the strain by eye, and a vet or laboratory is needed if this matters for your plan.
spread: Infected sheep carry the bacteria in their feet and drop them onto pasture, paths, yards and bedding wherever they walk.
Healthy sheep pick it up from contaminated ground, especially around water troughs, feeding areas, gateways, night bomas and muddy tracks where many feet pass.
Wet, warm conditions are the main trigger, so outbreaks usually build up during the long and short rains, when grass is long and wet and ground stays muddy.
The bacteria survive only a short time in the soil, generally from a few days up to about two weeks, so the real long-term source is chronically infected sheep, not the land itself.
Buying sheep from markets or other farms is a common way the disease enters a clean flock, because carrier sheep may look only slightly lame or not lame at all.
Sharing rams, communal grazing, shared dips and common watering points in pastoral and mixed systems allows spread between flocks.
Overgrown hooves, injuries from stones or thorns, and long periods standing in wet manure in poorly drained housing make infection easier to start.
Goats can also carry and suffer from foot rot, and cattle can carry some strains, so mixed herds can keep the problem going.
detail.atRisk: All ages of sheep can get foot rot, but adult sheep and older lambs on wet pasture are most often affected. Ewes heavy in late pregnancy and rams suffer badly because their weight presses on painful feet. Woolly breeds such as Merino and Dorper crosses and dairy-type breeds kept in damp conditions are commonly affected, though no breed is fully resistant, and local hair sheep like Red Maasai can also get it. Risk is highest during the long rains (March to May) and short rains (October to December), and in cool, high-rainfall areas such as parts of the Rift Valley, Central highlands and Mt Kenya and Aberdare regions. Flocks kept in muddy, poorly drained night bomas or zero-grazing pens with wet bedding, flocks grazing lush wet pastures, flocks bought in from markets, and pastoral flocks that share water points and grazing are all at higher risk.

early: Mild limping on one or more legs, often noticed first when the flock is moved or walks to water.
The sheep shifts weight from foot to foot when standing, or stands with a foot held slightly off the ground.
Skin between the claws looks red, swollen, wet and shiny, sometimes with a thin greyish-white layer on it.
Hair between the toes is lost and the area feels damp and warm compared with healthy feet.
A faint rotten smell when you lift and check the foot closely.
The sheep lags behind the flock and spends more time lying down.
advanced: Severe lameness, with the sheep refusing to put a foot down or walking on three legs.
Grazing on its knees because standing on the front feet is too painful.
Hoof horn lifting away from the heel, sole and sometimes the wall, with a grey, cheesy, very foul-smelling material underneath.
Loose flaps of horn that can be peeled back, exposing raw, sensitive tissue beneath.
Several feet affected, so the sheep lies down a lot and struggles to get up.
Weight loss, poor body condition and reduced wool growth because the animal cannot graze enough.
Rams refusing to mount and ewes losing condition or producing less milk for their lambs.
Maggots (fly strike) in neglected feet in warm weather, and misshapen, overgrown hooves in long-term chronic cases.

lookalikes.name: Foot scald (interdigital dermatitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Scald is inflammation of the skin between the toes only, with redness, moisture and mild to moderate lameness, but the hoof horn is not lifting off and the smell is mild. It is often the first stage of foot rot, so a flock with scald needs watching closely and should be checked by your vet.

lookalikes.name: Foot abscess
lookalikes.howToTell: An abscess usually affects only one claw on one foot of one sheep. The foot or coronet (the band just above the hoof) is hot, hard and swollen, and pus may burst out above the hoof. It does not normally spread through the flock the way foot rot does.

lookalikes.name: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)
lookalikes.howToTell: FMD causes sudden lameness in many animals at once, often with fever, blisters or raw sores in the mouth, on the gums, at the coronet and between the claws, and drooling or not eating. There is no underrun, smelly horn in the early stages. FMD is notifiable in Kenya, so if you see these signs, report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately.

lookalikes.name: Bluetongue
lookalikes.howToTell: Bluetongue is a viral disease spread by biting midges. It causes fever, a swollen face and lips, sores in the mouth, and a red or purple band at the coronet that makes sheep lame. The foot itself is not rotting and smelly, and the sheep is clearly sick all over, not just lame.

detail.diagnosis: Most vets diagnose foot rot by examining the feet carefully. They lift each foot, clean it, look between the claws and check whether the horn is lifting away, and they recognise the strong typical smell. Many vets give each foot a score from mild scald to severe underrunning, which helps decide treatment and which sheep to cull. Your vet will also look at the whole flock, because lameness can have other causes, and will rule out FMD, bluetongue, abscesses and injuries. Where it matters, for example before buying rams or when planning to eradicate the disease or vaccinate, the vet may take swabs from affected feet for laboratory testing to identify the bacteria and whether the strain is benign or virulent. Before the vet comes, you can help by penning the lame sheep in a clean, dry area, counting how many sheep are lame and how many feet are affected, noting when the lameness started, recording any recently bought or borrowed animals, and writing down any treatments or foot baths already used.
firstSteps: Catch every lame sheep and gently lift each foot to check between the claws and under the horn, so you know exactly how many animals and feet are affected.
Separate lame sheep from the healthy flock and keep them on clean, dry ground or in a pen with dry bedding, away from paths, water troughs and night bomas the healthy sheep use.
Make sure affected sheep can reach water, feed and shade easily without walking far, because pain stops them from competing with the flock.
Do not use any antibiotics, sprays or injections until your vet has examined the sheep and prescribed the right product, as wrong use can leave residues and breed resistance.
Avoid cutting away large amounts of horn or making feet bleed, because heavy paring delays healing and the cuttings and blood spread the bacteria to other sheep.
Wear gloves when handling infected feet, wash your hands afterwards, and clean knives, shears and boots so you do not carry the infection to healthy animals.
Write down the ear tag or description of each lame sheep, which feet are affected and the date, so you can follow their progress and identify repeat cases later.
Stop buying, selling or borrowing sheep, especially rams, until the problem is under control, and call your vet or the local veterinary office for advice.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment is decided and prescribed by a vet. For individual sheep with foot rot, vets commonly give an injectable antibiotic, often from groups such as tetracyclines (for example oxytetracycline), penicillins or macrolides. Some macrolides are dangerous to people if accidentally injected, so only a vet or trained person should handle them. A topical antibiotic spray, such as an oxytetracycline spray, is often used on the cleaned foot as well. The vet may also give an anti-inflammatory painkiller, such as meloxicam, so the sheep starts walking and eating again sooner. Affected sheep should be treated promptly, ideally within days of becoming lame, because early treatment works much better. Current advice is to avoid heavy foot trimming of infected feet; the vet may gently remove only loose, dead horn. For the flock, the vet may recommend foot bathing with products such as zinc sulphate, used at the strength and standing time on the label or advised by your vet. Formalin and copper sulphate are also used in some places, but both are hazardous to people, animals and the environment, and formalin is painful on raw feet. In some countries a multi-strain foot rot vaccine is available; availability in Kenya varies, so ask your vet. Most treated sheep improve within a few days to two weeks. Sheep that do not respond, or keep coming back lame, are usually advised for culling. All drugs have milk and meat withdrawal periods, which is the time you must wait before selling milk or slaughtering. Follow them exactly as stated on the label or by the vet. Antibiotics should only be used on sheep that truly need them, at the correct course, because overuse breeds antimicrobial resistance and makes future treatment harder for animals and people.
prevention: Quarantine all new or returning sheep for at least three to four weeks, check every foot on arrival and again before they join the flock, and do not buy sheep from flocks with a lameness problem.
Treat lame sheep quickly, ideally within a few days of lameness starting, so they shed fewer bacteria onto the pasture and are less likely to become chronic carriers.
Cull sheep that have been lame with foot rot repeatedly (for example two or more times in a season) or that do not respond to treatment, because these carriers keep reinfecting the flock.
Use foot baths as your vet advises, especially before and during the rains and after moving sheep. Let sheep stand on clean, dry ground afterwards and never let them drink from the bath.
Keep night bomas, pens and zero-grazing units well drained, raise or slat floors where possible, and change wet bedding often so feet stay dry.
Fill in or gravel muddy areas around water troughs, gates and feeding points, and move troughs regularly so mud does not build up.
Use clean ground management: after sheep with foot rot have been on a paddock, keep the flock off it for about two weeks if you can, so the bacteria in the soil die off.
Avoid routine heavy trimming of feet. Only lightly correct badly overgrown hooves, clean tools between sheep, and burn or bury the trimmings.
Ask your vet whether a foot rot vaccine is available and suitable for your flock, and whether lab testing of strains would help.
Keep good records of lameness by ear tag, and select breeding rams and ewes from animals that have stayed sound, since resistance to foot rot is partly inherited.
detail.impact: Foot rot is one of the most costly causes of lameness in sheep. Lame sheep graze less, so they lose weight and body condition, and lambs grow more slowly. Ewes with sore feet produce less milk and may have weaker lambs and lower fertility, while lame rams may refuse to mount, leading to fewer lambs and a spread-out lambing season. Wool growth and quality drop in woolled breeds. Thin, limping sheep fetch a poorer price at market, and buyers may avoid a flock with a known lameness problem. On top of this come the costs of vet visits, drugs, foot bath chemicals and a great deal of extra labour catching and checking sheep, plus income lost while waiting out drug withdrawal periods. Culling chronic carriers also means replacing breeding stock. For a smallholder with a small flock, a bad outbreak during the rains can wipe out much of the season's profit.
detail.humanHealth: Foot rot bacteria are not known to cause disease in people, so the infection itself is not a human health risk. The main risks come from treatment. Antibiotics used on sheep can leave residues in milk and meat, so always observe the withdrawal periods on the label or given by your vet before selling or eating milk or meat. Some injectable antibiotics used in sheep, such as certain macrolides, can be very dangerous or fatal if accidentally injected into a person, so only trained people should handle them. Foot bath chemicals are also hazardous: formalin irritates the eyes, skin and lungs and is linked to cancer, and copper sulphate is poisonous if swallowed. Wear gloves, boots and eye protection, keep children away from foot baths, and dispose of used solution safely away from water sources, as advised on the label.
detail.outlook: The outlook for individual sheep is generally good when foot rot is caught early and treated by a vet. Most respond within days to a couple of weeks and return to normal grazing. Recovery is slower and less certain when the horn is badly underrun, several feet are affected, the sheep has been lame for a long time, or it has developed fly strike or misshapen hooves. Some sheep become chronic carriers and keep relapsing; these rarely do well and are better culled. At flock level, foot rot can be greatly reduced, and in some flocks eliminated, if the farmer combines prompt treatment, culling of carriers, quarantine of new stock, foot bathing and dry housing. Success depends on doing this consistently, especially during the rains, rather than reacting only when many sheep are already lame.

faqs.q: Is foot rot the same as the limping my sheep get every rainy season?
faqs.a: Not always. Many sheep get mild redness between the toes, called scald, in wet weather, and this can heal when conditions dry out. True foot rot is when the horn starts lifting from the foot and there is a strong rotten smell. Scald can turn into foot rot if the D. nodosus bacterium is present in the flock. If lameness keeps coming back every rainy season and you smell rotting feet, ask your vet to check, because your flock likely carries foot rot.

faqs.q: Should I cut away all the rotten hoof to clean it out?
faqs.a: No. Older advice was to pare feet heavily, but research and current vet guidance show that cutting deep into the foot slows healing, causes pain and bleeding, and spreads bacteria on knives and ground. Your vet may gently remove only loose, dead horn. Prompt treatment prescribed by your vet works better than heavy trimming.

faqs.q: Can a foot bath alone cure foot rot?
faqs.a: A foot bath helps control spread and can help mild cases, but it is usually not enough on its own for sheep with underrun feet. Those sheep need examination and treatment prescribed by a vet. Foot baths work best as part of a plan: treat lame sheep promptly, cull repeat cases, quarantine new stock and keep housing dry. Always use foot bath chemicals at the strength on the label or as your vet advises, and let sheep stand on dry ground afterwards.

faqs.q: Why does my vet tell me to cull some of my sheep?
faqs.a: Some sheep never fully clear the infection. They carry the bacteria in their feet and keep spreading them every time the ground is wet, even if they look only slightly lame. These chronic carriers are the main reason foot rot stays on a farm year after year. Removing them, usually to slaughter after any drug withdrawal period is finished, protects the rest of the flock and saves you money on repeated treatment.

faqs.q: Can my goats or cattle catch foot rot from my sheep?
faqs.a: Goats can get foot rot and pass it to and from sheep, so if you keep both, treat them as one group for foot checks, foot baths and quarantine. Cattle can carry some strains of the bacteria without showing much disease, and they get their own different foot infections. Your vet can advise how to manage mixed herds.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for foot rot in Kenya?
faqs.a: Foot rot vaccines exist and are used in some countries, but there are many strains of the bacterium and the vaccine needs to match them. Availability in Kenya varies and may change, so ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer what is currently registered and whether it suits your flock. Even where a vaccine is used, it works alongside treatment, culling, quarantine and dry housing, not instead of them.

card.headline: Best, fastest-growing lamb found suddenly dead
card.look: A healthy-looking, well-fed lamb is found dead or dying, often after a change to lush pasture or more concentrate. A few are seen staggering, pressing their head against walls, frothing at the mouth or lying on their side paddling before death.
card.action: Cut back concentrates and move the flock off lush feed now, call your vet immediately, and do not open or eat any carcass until the vet has ruled out anthrax.

detail.summary: Enterotoxaemia, commonly called pulpy kidney, is a sudden and usually fatal poisoning of sheep caused by a toxin made by bacteria in the gut. It strikes the best-fed, fastest-growing lambs, often after a sudden change to richer feed, so many farmers lose their most valuable animals without warning. Treatment rarely works once signs appear, but the disease is almost completely preventable with regular clostridial vaccination and careful feeding.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Clostridium perfringens type D, a bacterium that normally lives in small numbers in the gut of healthy sheep and in soil. Clostridia are a group of bacteria that form tough spores and produce powerful toxins (poisons). When a sheep suddenly eats a lot of rich feed, such as grain, dairy meal, lush green pasture after rain, or a large amount of milk from a heavy-milking ewe, undigested starch and sugar spill over from the stomach into the small intestine. This sudden flood of food lets the bacteria multiply very fast. As they multiply, they release a toxin called epsilon toxin. The toxin is made in an inactive form and is switched on by digestive enzymes in the gut. It then passes through the gut wall into the blood. Epsilon toxin damages the lining of small blood vessels, so fluid leaks out into the tissues. This causes swelling of the brain, fluid around the heart and lungs, and damage to the kidneys. Brain damage explains the staggering, blindness and fits. The toxin also causes high blood sugar, so sugar appears in the urine. Because the toxin acts so quickly, most affected lambs die within a few hours, often before anyone notices they are ill. The kidneys of dead lambs soften very quickly after death, turning soft and pulpy, which gives the disease its common name.
spread: It is not passed from sheep to sheep like a contagious infection; the bacteria are already present in the gut and soil of almost every farm.
The main trigger is a sudden change to richer feed, such as starting or increasing dairy meal, maize, sorghum or other grain without a gradual build-up.
Moving sheep onto lush, fast-growing pasture after the long or short rains, or onto young irrigated grass, crop residues or green fodder, can set it off.
Lambs suckling heavy-milking ewes, especially single lambs that get all the milk, are at high risk because they take in large amounts of milk at once.
Irregular feeding, for example hungry sheep given a large meal after a delay, missed feeding days, or sheep breaking into a grain store or maize field, can trigger cases.
Stress from transport, weaning, drenching or sudden weather changes, combined with rich feed, increases the risk.
Heavy worm burdens and other gut upsets may slow gut movement and allow the bacteria to build up, though feed change remains the main cause.
Unvaccinated flocks, or lambs born to unvaccinated ewes, have no protection against the toxin and suffer the most losses.
detail.atRisk: The animals most at risk are fast-growing lambs, roughly from a few weeks old up to weaning, especially the biggest and best-fed in the flock. Single lambs on heavy-milking ewes, lambs given creep feed, and weaned lambs being fattened on concentrates for market (for example ahead of festive season sales) are classic victims. Adult sheep can also be affected when they are suddenly given grain or moved onto lush pasture, but this is less common. Lambs born to unvaccinated ewes are at much higher risk, because they receive no protective antibodies (defence proteins) in the colostrum, the first thick milk. In Kenya, cases often rise at the start of the long and short rains when pastures flush green, and in zero-grazing or semi-intensive units where dairy meal or grain is introduced quickly. Improved and exotic breeds such as Dorper, Merino, Hampshire Down and their crosses, which grow fast and are often fed more intensively, are frequently affected, but local Red Maasai and Blackhead Persian sheep are not immune if fed richly and left unvaccinated. Goats also get enterotoxaemia, often with more diarrhoea, and vaccines do not always protect them as strongly.

early: Most often there are no early signs at all, and the first thing the farmer sees is a well-grown lamb found dead in the morning, often lying on its side.
A lamb that is dull, stops suckling or eating, and separates itself from the flock shortly before collapsing.
Staggering, wobbling or walking in an uncoordinated way, as if drunk.
Apparent blindness, bumping into objects, or standing with the head pressed against a wall or fence.
Grinding of the teeth, drooling or froth around the mouth.
Some animals pass soft or greenish dung, though diarrhoea is not always present in sheep.
advanced: Lying on the side, unable to rise, with the legs paddling as if running.
Fits (convulsions), with the head and neck pulled backwards and the legs held stiff.
Fast or noisy breathing as fluid builds up around the lungs and heart.
Coma and death, usually within a few hours of the first signs, sometimes within minutes.
A carcass that bloats and decomposes quickly, especially in hot weather.
In the rarer slower form, usually in older sheep, wandering, blindness and head pressing may last a day or more, and a few animals survive with lasting brain damage.

lookalikes.name: Anthrax
lookalikes.howToTell: Anthrax also causes sudden death, but dark, tarry blood that does not clot may ooze from the nose, mouth or anus, the carcass may not stiffen normally, and it can affect sheep of any age and other species on the farm. Anthrax is notifiable and dangerous to people, so never open a carcass if anthrax is possible; let the vet decide and test first.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater (Cowdriosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Heartwater is spread by bont ticks (Amblyomma), so ticks are usually present and it is not linked to feed changes. Sheep often show high fever for a day or more, then nervous signs such as chewing movements, high-stepping and fits. At post-mortem both diseases can show fluid around the heart, so a vet's tests are needed to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Grain overload (rumen acidosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This follows the same trigger of eating too much grain, but affected sheep usually live longer, with a swollen left side, severe watery sour-smelling diarrhoea, dehydration and weakness over a day or two. The two conditions can happen together after a grain break-in, so the vet may treat both.

lookalikes.name: Polioencephalomalacia (vitamin B1 / thiamine-related brain disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Sheep show blindness, star-gazing, head pressing and fits similar to pulpy kidney, but signs often develop over one or more days rather than hours, and affected sheep can respond quickly to vitamin B1 treatment from a vet. Sugar in the urine points more towards enterotoxaemia.

detail.diagnosis: Because most lambs are found dead, diagnosis is usually made from the history and a post-mortem examination. The vet will ask about recent feed changes, the age and condition of the dead lambs, and the vaccination history of the ewes and lambs. In a live or freshly dead animal, the vet may test the urine for sugar, as high urine sugar is a strong clue. At post-mortem, typical findings include excess straw-coloured fluid with clots in the sac around the heart, small bleeding spots on the heart and gut, a full gut with rich feed, and soft, pulpy kidneys, although kidneys soften after death in many conditions so this alone is not proof. Confirmation needs laboratory tests that detect epsilon toxin in fluid from the small intestine, and sometimes tests to identify the type of Clostridium and microscope examination of the brain. Samples can be sent through your vet to the County Veterinary Laboratory, a Regional Veterinary Investigation Laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete. Before opening any carcass, the vet should rule out anthrax. To help the vet, keep the carcass cool and covered, away from dogs and scavengers, and do not cut it open yourself. Write down when each animal was last seen healthy, what it had been eating in the past week, any recent feed or pasture change, vaccination dates and products used, and how many animals are affected.
firstSteps: Call your vet or the County Veterinary Officer at once, because the remaining flock is at risk and quick advice can stop further deaths.
Immediately reduce or stop concentrates, dairy meal and grain, and give the flock good quality hay or mature grass instead, so the gut slows down.
Move the flock off lush, fast-growing pasture onto rougher, more mature grazing until the vet advises otherwise.
Make sure all sheep have clean drinking water and shade, and keep any sick lamb quiet in a cool, sheltered place where it cannot injure itself during fits.
Do not force liquids down the throat of a lamb that is down, fitting or cannot swallow, as it may choke or inhale the fluid.
Do not open, skin, eat or sell any animal that has died suddenly; cover it, keep dogs and children away, and wait for the vet to rule out anthrax.
Wear gloves when handling carcasses, wash your hands with soap afterwards, and dispose of carcasses by deep burial or burning as advised by the vet.
Record which lambs died, their ages, what they were fed and when, and check your vaccination records so you can share them with the vet.
detail.vetTreatment: Once clear signs appear, treatment usually fails because the toxin has already damaged the brain and blood vessels, so you should expect many affected lambs to die despite care. In lambs found early or in the slower form, a vet may give clostridial antitoxin (antibodies that neutralise the toxin) if it is available, though it can be difficult to find in Kenya. The vet may also use antibiotics such as penicillin to reduce bacterial growth in the gut, anti-inflammatory drugs, and fluids to support the circulation. For the rest of the flock, the most important action is usually to vaccinate all sheep with a clostridial vaccine straight away, even during an outbreak, and to change the feeding. Vaccine protection takes some days to develop, so feed changes are what protect the flock in the meantime. The vet may also give some lambs oral antibiotics short-term in a serious outbreak. All treatments must be prescribed by a vet. Antibiotics must only be used when truly needed and at the vet's direction, because misuse drives antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to drugs that people and animals rely on. Treated sheep must not be slaughtered for meat, and milk from treated ewes must not be used, until the withdrawal period on the product label has passed; ask your vet for the exact period.
prevention: Vaccinate every sheep with a multivalent clostridial vaccine (one that covers several clostridial diseases, including Clostridium perfringens type D) available from agrovets and vets, following the label and your vet's advice for the timing of doses.
Give previously unvaccinated sheep a full first course, which normally means two injections a few weeks apart, and then regular boosters; a single injection on its own gives poor protection.
Booster ewes a few weeks before lambing so that their colostrum carries strong protection to the lambs, and make sure every lamb suckles colostrum within the first hours of life.
Vaccinate lambs when the protection from their mothers starts to wear off, before weaning and before any move to concentrates or rich pasture, as guided by your vet and the vaccine label.
Introduce any concentrate, dairy meal, grain or new rich feed slowly over about two weeks, starting with small amounts and increasing gradually, and always provide good roughage such as hay.
Feed at regular times every day, split concentrates into two or more small feeds, and avoid letting hungry sheep gorge after a missed feed.
At the start of the long and short rains, limit time on very lush pasture at first, give hay before turning out, and move sheep gradually onto new green grazing.
Store grain, dairy meal and maize securely so sheep cannot break in, and keep a regular deworming programme guided by your vet to keep the gut healthy.
detail.impact: Pulpy kidney causes heavy financial losses because it kills the best lambs, the ones that were growing fastest and would fetch the highest price at market or be kept as breeding stock. On a smallholder farm with only a few sheep, losing two or three fat lambs can wipe out a season's income. For commercial and fattening units, sudden deaths in a pen of lambs on concentrates can be severe and disrupt sales plans, for example ahead of festive season demand. There are also costs for vet visits, laboratory tests and carcass disposal, and the meat cannot safely be sold or eaten. Repeated outbreaks discourage farmers from improving feeding, which holds back growth rates and farm productivity. Compared with these losses, clostridial vaccines are inexpensive, making prevention one of the best-value investments a sheep farmer can make.
detail.humanHealth: Clostridium perfringens type D enterotoxaemia in sheep is not considered a disease that spreads to people. However, any sheep that dies suddenly could have died of anthrax, which is very dangerous to humans, so never open, skin, eat, sell or give away the meat of a sheep that died suddenly until a vet has ruled anthrax out. Wear gloves when handling carcasses and wash hands well with soap. If sheep are treated with antibiotics or other drugs, do not sell or eat their meat or use milk until the withdrawal period on the label has ended, to avoid drug residues reaching people.
detail.outlook: For lambs that show signs of pulpy kidney, the outlook is poor, and most die within hours even with treatment. A small number found very early, or with the slower form, may survive with vet treatment, but some are left with lasting brain damage, poor growth or blindness and may need to be culled. For the flock as a whole, the outlook is very good once feeding is corrected and all sheep are properly vaccinated with boosters; new cases usually stop within days of feed changes and vaccination taking effect. Well-vaccinated flocks with steady, gradual feeding rarely see this disease.

faqs.q: Why does pulpy kidney always seem to kill my best lambs?
faqs.a: The disease is triggered by large amounts of rich feed or milk reaching the gut. The lambs that eat or drink the most, and grow the fastest, are exactly the ones that give the bacteria the most food to multiply and make toxin. That is why the biggest, healthiest-looking lambs are often the ones found dead, while thinner lambs are spared.

faqs.q: I vaccinated my ewes, so why did a lamb still die?
faqs.a: Protection from the ewe's colostrum only lasts for a limited time, so older lambs need their own vaccination. Also, ewes need a full first course plus a booster before lambing for strong protection, and lambs must suckle colostrum early. Vaccine that was stored out of the fridge, expired or given incorrectly may not work. Ask your vet to review your vaccination programme, and remember that even a good programme works best with gradual feed changes.

faqs.q: Can I treat pulpy kidney myself with antibiotics from the agrovet?
faqs.a: No. Once signs appear, antibiotics alone rarely save the lamb, because the damage is done by a toxin, not just by the bacteria. Using antibiotics without a vet's prescription can waste money, leave drug residues in meat and milk, and add to antimicrobial resistance. Call your vet, who can decide whether treatment is worth trying and, most importantly, protect the rest of the flock.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat a sheep that died of pulpy kidney?
faqs.a: You should not eat or sell any sheep that died suddenly. You cannot tell by looking whether the death was pulpy kidney or anthrax, and anthrax can kill people. Even if a vet confirms enterotoxaemia, a sheep that died of illness is not fit for human food. Dispose of the carcass as your vet advises.

faqs.q: Should I vaccinate during an outbreak, or will it make things worse?
faqs.a: Vaccinating the whole flock during an outbreak is normally recommended by vets, because it builds protection for the animals that are still healthy. Protection takes some days to develop, so at the same time you must cut back rich feed and give more roughage. Your vet may also advise extra measures for high-risk lambs.

faqs.q: Do my goats need the same vaccine?
faqs.a: Goats also get enterotoxaemia and can be vaccinated with clostridial vaccines, but their protection tends to be shorter, so vets often advise more frequent boosters for goats than for sheep. Check the vaccine label to confirm it is approved for goats, and ask your vet for a programme that suits your herd.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can support hydration in a lamb that is recovering, alert and able to drink normally, used only alongside vet treatment and on the vet's advice; it does not treat the toxin, should never be forced into a lamb that is down or fitting, and does not replace clostridial vaccination and careful feeding.
