card.headline: Damp, smelly wool with crawling maggots
card.look: A patch of wet, brownish, foul-smelling wool, usually around the tail, breech or a wound, with cream-coloured maggots at the skin. The sheep is restless, stamps its feet, twitches its tail and keeps turning to bite or rub the spot.
card.action: Catch and isolate the sheep today, gently clip the wool around the patch so air reaches the skin, and call your vet at once, because fly strike can kill within days.

aka: Screwworm infestation (when Old World screwworm is involved)
detail.summary: Fly strike happens when flies lay eggs on a sheep's soiled wool or open wound and the hatching maggots feed on the living skin and flesh. It can start within hours of eggs being laid and gets worse very fast, causing pain, poisoning of the blood and death if missed. It is common in Kenya and East Africa, especially in warm, wet weather during the long and short rains. Daily checks and good flock management prevent most cases.
detail.cause: Fly strike is caused by the maggots (larvae) of certain flies. Blowflies, the shiny green, blue or bronze flies often seen around rubbish and dead animals, are attracted to the smell of wet wool soiled with dung or urine, rotting skin and wounds. They lay clusters of tiny eggs there. In warm, humid conditions the eggs hatch quickly into maggots that scrape and eat the skin, releasing digestive juices that dissolve tissue. This creates a raw, wet wound that smells even stronger and attracts more flies, so the strike spreads. In East Africa the Old World screwworm fly (Chrysomya bezziana) is also a concern: it lays eggs in fresh wounds, navels of newborn lambs, castration or docking wounds and tick-bite sores, and its maggots bore deep into healthy flesh. As maggots feed, poisons and bacteria from the damaged tissue get into the blood. This causes fever, dehydration, loss of appetite and a condition called toxaemia (blood poisoning), which is what usually kills struck sheep.
spread: Wool soiled with diarrhoea (scouring) is the most common trigger; scouring is often caused by worms, lush wet-season grazing or sudden diet change.
Urine-stained wool around the rear of ewes, and around the sheath (pizzle) of rams and wethers, attracts flies.
Fresh wounds from castration, tail docking, ear notching, shearing cuts, fighting rams, thorns, dog bites or barbed wire are prime sites, especially for screwworm.
Navels of newborn lambs and the rear of ewes after lambing are attractive to egg-laying flies.
Damp fleece after rain, or wool affected by footrot discharge or skin infections such as lumpy wool, gives flies a moist place to lay eggs.
Dead animals, afterbirths and rubbish left lying around the farm breed large numbers of blowflies close to the flock.
Fly strike is not contagious from sheep to sheep, but one struck sheep produces maggots that drop to the ground and become new flies, raising the risk for the whole flock.
detail.atRisk: Any sheep can be struck, but risk is highest in woolly breeds and crosses such as Merino, Corriedale, Hampshire Down and Dorper crosses with long, dense wool around the breech. Hair sheep like Red Maasai and Blackhead Persian are less prone to body strike but still get wound and navel strike. Sheep with diarrhoea from worms, long undocked tails with dags (dung balls), heavy wrinkly skin, footrot, or any wound are at greatest risk. Young lambs with fresh navels, freshly castrated or docked lambs, and ewes around lambing are especially vulnerable. The danger peaks in warm, humid weather during and just after the long rains (March to May) and short rains (October to December). Zero-grazed sheep kept on wet, dirty bedding, and pastoral flocks that are not handled closely every day, are both at risk because cases can go unnoticed.

early: The sheep is restless, stamps its feet, shakes its tail and keeps turning its head to bite or nibble at its tail, flank or shoulder.
It rubs against posts, fences or other sheep and may walk away from the flock or lie down and get up repeatedly.
A patch of wool looks damp, darker or yellow-brown, often around the tail and breech, along the back, at the sheath or around a wound.
You notice a sour, rotten smell when you get close, even before you see maggots.
Flies keep landing and buzzing around one spot on the sheep.
When you part the wool, you see small cream maggots moving at the skin, or clusters of tiny white eggs on the wool.
advanced: A large wet, raw area with wool falling out or easily pulled away, and many maggots moving in the wound.
A strong, foul smell of rotting flesh that can be noticed from some distance.
Deep holes or pockets in the flesh, especially in wounds and navels, which suggests screwworm maggots burrowing in.
The sheep stops eating and drinking, stands hunched with its head down, or lies apart from the flock.
Fast breathing, weakness, staggering and inability to keep up with the flock.
Sunken eyes and dry mouth from dehydration, and finally collapse and death from blood poisoning if not treated.

lookalikes.name: Sheep scab or mange (mites)
lookalikes.howToTell: Scab also makes sheep itchy, rub and lose wool, but it spreads through the flock over weeks, causes crusty, scaly skin and tufts of wool pulling out, and has no maggots or rotten smell. Fly strike is usually in one or a few sheep, comes on fast, and you can see maggots in wet wool.

lookalikes.name: Lice and keds
lookalikes.howToTell: Lice and keds cause itching, rubbing and ragged wool, but the wool is not wet and smelly. Keds are wingless brown insects you can see crawling in the fleece; there are no maggots eating into the skin.

lookalikes.name: Lumpy wool (dermatophilosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This skin infection after heavy rain causes hard crusts and lumps of matted wool along the back, but no maggots and no rapid illness. However, these damp crusty areas can later be struck by flies, so check them closely.

lookalikes.name: Footrot
lookalikes.howToTell: Footrot also has a foul smell, but it comes from the feet and the sheep is lame. If the smell is from the wool or a body wound and the sheep is biting at its body, think fly strike. Footrot discharge on the legs can itself attract flies.

detail.diagnosis: Fly strike is usually confirmed simply by finding maggots on a careful examination. The vet will catch the sheep, part and clip the wool, and check the whole body, including the breech, tail, sheath, navel, feet, horns and any wounds, because there may be more than one strike site. They will judge how deep the damage goes, check temperature, hydration and general condition, and decide whether the sheep is suffering from toxaemia. If maggots are burrowing deep into healthy flesh, the vet may collect some larvae in a small container with alcohol to identify the fly species, especially if screwworm is suspected or the case is unusual. The vet will also look for the underlying cause, such as worm-related scouring or footrot. To help, keep the sheep in a clean, shaded pen, note when you first saw the signs, record any recent castration, docking, shearing or wounds, list any products you have already applied, and be ready to show the vet other sheep in the flock.
firstSteps: Catch the struck sheep and separate it in a clean, shaded, fly-protected pen or shed so it can be handled and watched closely.
Wear gloves and wash your hands well afterwards, because maggots, pus and dirty wool carry bacteria, and screwworm can also infest human wounds.
Using clean shears or scissors, gently clip the wool well beyond the edge of the damp patch so the skin can dry and you can see how far the strike has spread.
Pick off visible maggots and collect them with the clipped wool into a bag or tin, then burn or bury it deeply so they cannot turn into new flies.
Do not pour diesel, kerosene, engine oil, battery acid or strong disinfectant on the wound; these burn the skin, cause pain and poisoning, and slow healing.
Give the sheep clean fresh water and soft, palatable feed, and keep it calm and out of the sun.
Check every other sheep in the flock the same day, especially those with dirty breeches, wounds or diarrhoea, because flies will be active across the group.
Call your vet or animal health assistant today, record what you saw and found, and do not apply any insecticide or give any medicine until the vet advises which product is safe for sheep.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be done or prescribed by a vet, who will choose products registered for sheep in Kenya. The vet first clips the wool widely around the strike, removes as many maggots as possible, and cleans the wound with a mild antiseptic. They then apply a larvicide or insecticide (a product that kills maggots) to the wound and surrounding skin. Common active ingredients used on sheep include spinosad, cyromazine, dicyclanil, ivermectin, and synthetic pyrethroids such as cypermethrin or deltamethrin; older organophosphates such as diazinon are also used in some places but are more toxic to people and animals. The vet may also apply a fly-repellent wound dressing to stop re-strike. If the sheep is weak, feverish or has deep wounds, the vet may give pain relief (an anti-inflammatory drug) and may decide antibiotics are needed to control infection and toxaemia; antibiotics should only be used when a vet judges them necessary and the full course must be completed, because misuse drives antimicrobial resistance. Very sick sheep may need fluids to correct dehydration. All of these drugs have meat and milk withdrawal periods, which are times you must wait before slaughtering or using milk; ask your vet and follow the label exactly. Expect to check and possibly re-treat the wound for several days until it is dry and healing. Severe cases with collapse may not recover, and the vet may advise humane euthanasia to prevent suffering.
prevention: Inspect every sheep closely at least once a day during the rains and warm weather, looking at the tail, breech, sheath and any wounds, and watching for sheep biting at themselves or standing apart.

Control worms with a vet-guided plan, using faecal egg counts or the FAMACHA eye-colour check where possible, so sheep do not scour and soil their wool; avoid unnecessary deworming that leads to drug resistance.
Crutch (clip the wool around the tail and breech) and remove dags before the rains, and shear on time so wool is not long and dirty in the high-risk season.
Have tail docking and castration done correctly by a trained person, ideally in cooler, drier weather, and treat and check these wounds daily until healed.
Treat the navels of newborn lambs with a vet-recommended antiseptic soon after birth, and keep lambing areas clean and dry.
Ask your vet or agrovet about preventive fly-strike products registered for sheep in Kenya, such as long-acting pour-ons, and apply them before the high-risk season, respecting withdrawal periods.
Treat wounds, footrot, skin infections and tick bites promptly, and use good tick control, since every sore is an invitation to flies.
Bury or burn dead animals, afterbirths and slaughter waste quickly, keep manure heaps away from sheep pens, and change wet bedding often in zero-grazing units.
Use fly traps around the sheep yard if available, and when buying breeding stock consider animals with less wool and fewer skin wrinkles around the breech.
detail.impact: Fly strike causes direct losses through death of sheep, sometimes valuable breeding ewes or rams. Animals that survive lose weight and body condition quickly because of pain and poor feeding, which lowers their market price at sale or at the livestock market. Ewes may lose their lambs or produce less milk for them, and rams may be out of service for weeks. Wool from struck areas is stained and damaged, and skins can be scarred, lowering hide value. Farmers also face costs for vet visits, insecticides, wound dressings and the extra labour of daily inspections and treatments. On smallholder farms where a few sheep are an important savings bank, losing even one animal can be a serious setback.
detail.humanHealth: Fly strike itself does not pass from sheep to people, but the same flies, especially the Old World screwworm, can lay eggs in human wounds, so cover any cuts and wear gloves when handling struck sheep, then wash your hands with soap. Maggot-infested wounds contain bacteria that can infect people, so do not touch your face while working and wash clothes afterwards. Many insecticides used on sheep, particularly organophosphates and pyrethroids, are harmful to people if they touch the skin, are breathed in or are swallowed; wear gloves and long sleeves, follow the label, and keep products away from children, food and water sources. Drug and insecticide residues can remain in meat and milk, so always respect the withdrawal period on the label or as advised by your vet before slaughtering, selling or consuming products from a treated sheep.
detail.outlook: When fly strike is found early, while the patch is small and the sheep is still eating, the outlook is good and most sheep recover well with clipping, maggot removal and vet-advised treatment. Recovery becomes less certain as the wound gets larger and deeper, especially with screwworm maggots burrowing into flesh or strikes in several places. Sheep that have stopped eating, are weak, dehydrated or lying down have toxaemia and a guarded to poor chance of survival, even with good treatment. Recovered sheep can be struck again if the cause, such as scouring, dirty wool or an unhealed wound, is not fixed, so follow-up checks are important. Fast action is the single biggest factor in saving the animal.

faqs.q: Can I use diesel, kerosene or used engine oil to kill the maggots?
faqs.a: Please do not. These are still commonly used in some areas, but they burn and damage the skin, cause great pain, can be absorbed and poison the sheep, and make the wound slower to heal. They also contaminate the meat. Clip the wool, remove the maggots by hand, keep the sheep clean and shaded, and get a vet to apply a proper sheep-registered larvicide.

faqs.q: I picked out all the maggots I could see. Is the sheep now safe?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Maggots often hide deeper in the wool or burrow into pockets in the flesh, and flies will return to lay more eggs on the raw wound. Clip the area widely, look carefully again, and have the vet treat the wound with a product that kills remaining maggots and protects against re-strike. Check the sheep every day until the wound is dry and healing.

faqs.q: Why do the same sheep keep getting fly strike?
faqs.a: Repeated strikes usually point to an underlying problem, such as diarrhoea from worms, dags of dung under a long tail, urine staining, footrot, wrinkly skin or slow-healing wounds. Work with your vet to fix the cause: a proper worm control plan, crutching, good wound care and, if needed, a preventive product before the rains. Sheep that are struck again and again may be better culled from a breeding flock.

faqs.q: Is fly strike contagious? Should I worry about the rest of my flock?
faqs.a: It does not spread directly from sheep to sheep like an infection. However, the weather and flies that caused one strike are affecting all your sheep, and maggots from a struck sheep drop to the ground and become more flies. When you find one case, check every sheep the same day and destroy all removed maggots and wool by burning or deep burial.

faqs.q: My sheep are Red Maasai and Dorper, not woolly Merinos. Do I still need to worry?
faqs.a: Yes. Hair sheep and Dorpers are less likely to get body strike in soiled wool, but they still get strike in wounds, castration and docking sites, tick-bite sores, fighting injuries and the navels of young lambs, and screwworm attacks such wounds in any breed. Daily checks and prompt wound care are important for every breed.

faqs.q: When can I sell or eat a sheep that has been treated for fly strike?
faqs.a: Only after the withdrawal period of every product used has passed. Insecticides, larvicides, antibiotics and pain relief drugs all leave residues in meat and milk for a set time. Ask your vet for the withdrawal period, write down the date of the last treatment, and do not slaughter or sell before it is over, even if the sheep looks fully well.

products.role: Struck sheep often stop drinking and become dehydrated and weak, especially in hot weather. RE-COVER oral rehydration solution can be offered in clean drinking water, with your vet's agreement, to help replace fluids and salts and support the sheep while it recovers. It does not kill maggots or treat the wound and must be used alongside the vet's wound treatment and good management.

card.headline: Pregnant ewe standing alone, dull and blind
card.look: A heavily pregnant ewe, often carrying twins, stops eating and stands apart from the flock. She may stare upwards (star-gazing), bump into things as if blind, grind her teeth or tremble, and later lie down and be unable to get up.
card.action: Move her to a quiet, sheltered pen with water and good feed, and call your vet immediately, because every hour counts.

detail.summary: Pregnancy toxaemia is a metabolic disease of ewes in the last four to six weeks of pregnancy. The growing lambs, especially twins or triplets, need more energy than the ewe can get from her feed. Her body breaks down its own fat too fast, her blood sugar falls and toxic by-products build up, damaging her liver and brain. It is an emergency: without fast treatment many ewes die, and the lambs are often lost too.
detail.cause: In the last six weeks of pregnancy, the lambs inside the ewe grow very quickly and take a large share of the sugar (glucose) in her blood. At the same time, the swollen womb presses on her stomach, so she physically cannot eat as much. If her feed is poor, scarce or suddenly cut, she goes into negative energy balance, meaning she uses more energy than she takes in. Her body then breaks down stored fat for fuel. The liver cannot process this flood of fat properly, so fat builds up in the liver (fatty liver) and substances called ketones are released into the blood. Ketones are acids that make the ewe feel sick and stop eating even more, which worsens the problem in a vicious circle. Low blood sugar and high ketones starve and poison the brain, which is why she becomes dull, blind and wobbly. In late stages the kidneys also suffer, the lambs may die inside her, and their decay can poison her further. The disease is not caused by a germ and is not contagious; it is caused by a mismatch between what the ewe needs and what she gets.
spread: It does not spread from animal to animal; several ewes falling sick at once usually means the whole flock is underfed in late pregnancy.
Poor or dried-up pasture in the dry season, or during drought, is a common trigger when ewes are due to lamb at that time.
Carrying twins or triplets greatly increases the energy demand and the risk.
Sudden feed changes, missed feeds or a break in supplementation can tip a borderline ewe into disease within a day or two.
Stress such as long treks to water or grazing, transport, handling, shearing, dog attacks, heavy rain and cold, or a sudden change of pen can stop a ewe eating and set it off.
Other illness that reduces appetite, such as heavy worm burdens (especially wireworm, Haemonchus), foot rot or lameness, or bad teeth, makes it much more likely.
Ewes that are too fat in early pregnancy and then lose condition quickly in late pregnancy are at very high risk, as are very thin ewes with no reserves.
detail.atRisk: Ewes in the last four to six weeks of pregnancy are at risk, especially those carrying twins or triplets. Very fat ewes and very thin ewes are both at high risk, as are older ewes with worn teeth and first-time mothers that are still growing. Breeds and flocks that often have twins, such as Dorper and well-fed crossbred flocks, see it more often, though Red Maasai and other local breeds can be affected when feed runs short. In Kenya the danger is highest when late pregnancy falls in the dry months before the long or short rains, or during drought in pastoral areas where ewes walk long distances. Zero-grazed or semi-intensive ewes fed mainly on poor hay, maize stover or cut grass without supplements are also at risk. Goats get the same disease (pregnancy toxaemia in does).

early: The ewe separates from the flock, lags behind when the flock moves, or is slow to come for feed.
She eats less or refuses concentrates, and may pick at feed without swallowing much.
She looks dull and sleepy, with drooping ears and head, and seems uninterested in her surroundings.
She may seem not to see well, walking into fences, water troughs or other sheep.
Her breath or urine may smell sweet, fruity or like nail-polish remover; this is the smell of ketones.
Fine muscle tremors may be seen around the head, ears or lips, and she may grind her teeth.
advanced: Star-gazing: she holds her head up and back, staring at the sky, or presses her head against a wall or fence.
Clear blindness: she does not blink or flinch when a hand moves towards her eyes.
Staggering, walking in circles, twitching or full convulsions (fits).
Lying down on her chest and being unable or unwilling to stand, often with her head turned to her flank.
Constipation with small, dry droppings, and a fast, shallow breathing pattern.
Coma, where she lies on her side and does not respond, usually followed by death within a few days if untreated.
The lambs may die inside her; she may abort or, if she lambs, the lambs are often weak or dead.

lookalikes.name: Hypocalcaemia (milk fever in ewes)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is low blood calcium and also hits ewes in late pregnancy, often after stress, yarding or a sudden feed change. It comes on faster, often within hours, and several ewes may go down together. Affected ewes are usually weak and wobbly rather than blind, and they respond quickly, often within an hour, to calcium given by a vet. The two conditions often occur together, which is why vets commonly treat for both.

lookalikes.name: Polioencephalomalacia (CCN, thiamine or vitamin B1 deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: This also causes blindness, star-gazing and fits, but it can affect sheep of any age and sex, including young growing lambs and rams, not just pregnant ewes. It is often linked to sudden diet changes to rich concentrate feeds. Animals usually improve after a vet gives thiamine.

lookalikes.name: Listeriosis (circling disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial infection, often linked to spoiled silage, typically causes one-sided signs: a drooping ear, eyelid or lip on one side, drooling, and walking in circles in one direction. It can affect any sheep, and there may be fever, which is not typical of twin lamb disease.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater
lookalikes.howToTell: This tick-borne disease, common in many parts of Kenya, causes high fever, high-stepping walk, chewing movements, fits and sudden death in sheep of any age. Ticks are usually present and the animal has a fever, whereas a ewe with twin lamb disease usually has a normal or low temperature and the problem is tied to late pregnancy.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will usually suspect pregnancy toxaemia from the history: a ewe in late pregnancy, often with twins, that has gone off feed and become dull or blind. They will examine her, check her temperature (usually normal or low), smell her breath, and feel or scan her belly for multiple lambs and check whether the lambs are alive. A simple urine or blood test can confirm high ketone levels; vets often use blood ketone meters or urine dipsticks on the farm. Blood tests may also check sugar and calcium, because low calcium often occurs at the same time. If a ewe has died, a post-mortem usually shows a pale, swollen, yellow fatty liver and two or more lambs in the womb. To help the vet, note when she was mated or when lambing is expected, how long she has been ill, what she has been fed over the last month, any recent stress or feed change, her body condition, recent deworming, and whether any other ewes are dull or eating less.
firstSteps: Separate the ewe into a quiet, dry, sheltered pen close to the flock so she can still see or hear other sheep, which reduces stress.
Offer clean, fresh water and her favourite feeds, such as fresh green grass, good hay, and a small amount of the concentrate she is used to; do not suddenly give her large amounts of grain.
If she is lying down, prop her up on her chest with bales or sacks so she can breathe and belch properly, and turn her to the other side every few hours to prevent bloat and muscle damage.

Call your vet or the nearest animal health officer immediately; early treatment saves far more ewes than late treatment. Ask on the phone whether to start an oral energy drench while you wait, and only give it if the vet advises and she can swallow normally.
Do not force liquids into a ewe that cannot swallow or is lying flat, because fluid can go into her lungs and kill her.
Check every other pregnant ewe in the flock today, look for any that are dull, slow or off feed, and improve feeding for the whole group straight away.
Write down her expected lambing date, the signs you see and when they started, and everything she has eaten, to share with the vet.
Prepare for a possible early or difficult lambing: have a clean, warm area, clean water and towels ready, and a way to feed colostrum (first milk) to weak lambs.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet, and the earlier it starts the better it works. In early cases, the vet usually gives an energy source by mouth, most commonly propylene glycol or glycerol drenches, sometimes with glucose-forming supplements, to raise blood sugar and slow fat breakdown. Many vets also give glucose (dextrose) solution into the vein, and calcium, because low calcium so often occurs at the same time. Supportive care may include B vitamins, fluids for dehydration, and an anti-inflammatory painkiller to help the ewe start eating again. The most effective way to remove the cause is often to end the pregnancy, because once the lambs are out the energy drain stops. Depending on how close she is to lambing and whether the lambs are alive, the vet may give a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone to bring on lambing within a day or two, or perform a caesarean section in suitable cases; lambs born early may be weak and need extra care and colostrum. In some cases the vet may use other hormones, such as insulin, under close supervision. Antibiotics do not treat pregnancy toxaemia itself; they are only used if the vet finds an infection, such as after a dead lamb or a caesarean, and should be used exactly as prescribed to avoid antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to medicines). Any drugs given, including corticosteroids, anti-inflammatories and antibiotics, carry milk and meat withdrawal periods, so ask your vet how long to wait before selling or eating meat or milk. Expect several days of nursing; ewes that respond usually start eating within one to three days.
prevention: Feed for the lambs she is carrying: raise the quality of feed steadily over the last six weeks of pregnancy, for example good hay or fresh pasture plus a gradually increasing amount of a concentrate such as sheep, dairy or ewe meal, maize germ or a protein cake like cotton seed or sunflower cake, as advised by your extension officer or vet.

Use body condition scoring, a simple hands-on check of fat over the backbone and loin on a scale of 1 (very thin) to 5 (very fat); aim for ewes in moderate condition, around score 3, at mating and through pregnancy, and avoid both fat and thin ewes.

Where possible, have ewes scanned by ultrasound around mid-pregnancy so twin-bearing ewes can be grouped and fed more; if scanning is not available, feed larger and older proven twin-bearers more generously.
Plan mating so that late pregnancy and lambing fall when pasture is best, often during or just after the long or short rains, and store hay or silage for late-pregnant ewes in dry periods.
Make changes to feed gradually over a week or more, never cut feed suddenly in late pregnancy, and give enough trough space so shy or timid ewes can eat too.

Keep worm burdens low with a planned deworming programme guided by your vet, ideally using FAMACHA eye-colour checks for wireworm, and treat foot rot and lameness promptly so ewes can graze and reach feed.
Reduce stress in late pregnancy: avoid long treks, rough handling, transport, shearing and dog attacks, and provide shelter from cold rain and strong wind.
Check teeth of older ewes and cull or give softer feed to broken-mouthed ewes; provide clean water close by and a suitable sheep mineral lick.
detail.impact: Twin lamb disease can be very costly for a Kenyan sheep farmer because it hits the most valuable animals at the most valuable time. A heavily pregnant ewe carrying twins represents her own value plus the value of two lambs for sale or breeding. Advanced cases often die, and even when the ewe is saved the lambs may be lost or born weak. Survivors may have poor milk, reject their lambs, or take a long time to regain condition, delaying the next mating. Vet visits, drugs and nursing time add cost. When several ewes fall sick together it is a sign the whole flock is underfed, and lambing percentage, weaning weights and flock growth all suffer. In pastoral areas during drought, losses can be heavy across many households at once.
detail.humanHealth: Pregnancy toxaemia is not infectious and cannot pass to people. The only human concern is drug residues: ewes treated with corticosteroids, anti-inflammatories, antibiotics or other medicines must not be slaughtered for meat, or their milk used, until the withdrawal period your vet gives has passed. Do not slaughter a sick or dying ewe for home use without a meat inspector's or vet's approval.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends strongly on how early treatment starts. Ewes treated in the early stage, while they are still standing and eating a little, often recover well, especially if lambing is close or is brought on by the vet. Once a ewe is lying down, blind, fitting or in a coma, the outlook is poor and many die even with good treatment. If the lambs have already died inside her, the risk to the ewe is higher. Removing the lambs early, by induced lambing or caesarean, usually gives the ewe the best chance, though early lambs may be weak. Ewes that recover can lamb normally in later pregnancies if they are kept in good condition and fed well in late pregnancy.

faqs.q: Is twin lamb disease contagious? Will my other ewes catch it?
faqs.a: No, it does not spread from sheep to sheep. But if one ewe has it, others in the same group are often close to getting it, because they are usually on the same feed. Treat one case as a warning for the whole flock: check all late-pregnant ewes and improve their feeding straight away.

faqs.q: My ewe was fat, so why did she get it? I thought it was only thin ewes.
faqs.a: Fat ewes are actually at high risk. They often eat less in late pregnancy because fat inside the belly and the big womb leave little room for the stomach, and when they break down their large fat stores the liver gets overloaded. Very thin ewes are also at risk because they have no reserves. The safest ewe is in moderate condition, not fat and not thin.

faqs.q: Can I just give her molasses or sugar water?
faqs.a: Molasses and sugar may help a little as a feed for ewes that are still eating, but they are not reliable treatment for a sick ewe, and forcing liquids into a weak ewe can cause choking or pneumonia. Call your vet, who may recommend a proper energy drench such as propylene glycol and give glucose and calcium directly. For prevention, molasses can be part of a balanced late-pregnancy ration.

faqs.q: Will the lambs survive?
faqs.a: It depends on how sick the ewe is and how close she is to lambing. In early cases near term, lambs are often born alive, especially if the vet brings on lambing. In advanced cases, lambs frequently die inside the ewe. Lambs born early or from sick ewes are often weak, so keep them warm, make sure they get colostrum within the first hours, and be ready to bottle-feed if the ewe has little milk.

faqs.q: Do goats get the same disease?
faqs.a: Yes. Does (female goats) carrying twins or triplets get pregnancy toxaemia in the same way, with the same signs and the same need for fast vet treatment. The same prevention applies: good feeding in late pregnancy, moderate body condition and low stress.

faqs.q: Will a ewe that recovered get it again next time?
faqs.a: She is not immune, and a ewe that tends to carry twins may be at risk again. With good body condition, planned feeding in the last six weeks and less stress, she can lamb safely next time. Some farmers choose to cull ewes that were badly affected, had poor milk or are old with worn teeth.

products.role: Can be used as a supportive aid for liver function and digestive stress during recovery, since twin lamb disease overloads the liver with fat; use only alongside the vet's treatment and better late-pregnancy feeding, never as a substitute for them.

An oral rehydration solution that can help keep a recovering ewe drinking and hydrated, but only if she is alert and swallowing normally and your vet agrees; it does not replace the energy, glucose or calcium treatment the vet gives.

pregnancy-toxaemia.seoDescription: Twin lamb disease in sheep: spot dullness, star-gazing and blindness in late-pregnant ewes, act fast, and learn feeding steps to prevent it in Kenya.

card.headline: Rubbing, biting and ragged wool loss
card.look: Sheep rub hard against posts, fences and walls, bite or pull at their own wool, and leave tufts behind. Underneath, the skin may be red and moist with yellow crusts, or the fleece may look thin, matted and tatty.
card.action: Separate the itchy sheep, check the rest of the flock by parting the wool, and call your vet or animal health officer to confirm whether it is scab or lice before buying any dip.

aka: Upele (Swahili, general term for mange or itchy skin disease)
detail.summary: Sheep scab is an intensely itchy skin disease caused by a tiny mite, Psoroptes ovis, that lives on the skin surface under the wool. Lice are small insects that live their whole life in the fleece and also cause itching, rubbing and damaged wool. Both spread quickly through a flock, make sheep lose condition, and spoil wool and skins. Scab in particular can become severe and can kill weak sheep and lambs if left untreated, so early action saves money and animals.
detail.cause: Sheep scab is caused by the mite Psoroptes ovis, which is barely visible to the naked eye. The mite does not burrow into the skin. Instead it lives on the surface, pierces the skin with its mouthparts and feeds on fluid. Its droppings and saliva trigger a strong allergic reaction, so the skin becomes inflamed, leaks fluid and forms yellow, wet, then crusty scabs. The mites move outwards to the healthy edge of the sore, so the patch keeps growing. The itching is so severe that sheep rub, scratch and bite until they tear out wool and damage the skin, and badly affected sheep stop grazing, lose weight and can collapse or even have fits. Lice are different. Chewing (biting) lice, mainly Bovicola ovis, feed on skin scurf and debris, while sucking lice (Linognathus species) feed on blood, mostly on the legs and face. Both irritate the skin and make sheep rub and bite. Heavy sucking-louse burdens can cause anaemia, which means too little blood. Lice damage is usually slower and less dramatic than scab, but large numbers cause poor wool, weight loss and hide damage.
spread: Direct contact between sheep is the main route, especially when animals are crowded together in night bomas, holding pens, trucks or at markets.
Buying in new sheep, rams or lambs that carry mites or lice is the most common way a clean flock becomes infected.
Scab mites can survive off the sheep for around two weeks, sometimes a little longer, so shared pens, rubbing posts, fences, shearing equipment and trucks can pass them on.
Wool tufts left on fences and thorn bushes can carry living mites to other sheep that rub on the same spot.
Lice survive only a short time off the sheep, so they mainly spread by sheep-to-sheep contact, but shared shearing equipment and handling pens can also play a part.
Mixing flocks at communal grazing, watering points and dips spreads both parasites, which is common in pastoral and group-ranch systems.
Scab can also spread from sheep to goats in some cases, so mixed flocks of sheep and goats should be watched together.
Failed or partial treatment, such as spraying only part of the flock or using the wrong product, leaves survivors that rebuild the infestation.
detail.atRisk: All ages of sheep can be affected, but woolled breeds such as Merino, Corriedale, Romney Marsh, Hampshire Down and Dorper crosses with longer wool show more damage than hair sheep like the Red Maasai or Blackhead Persian, which can still carry and suffer from mites and lice. Lambs, old ewes, thin sheep and heavily pregnant or nursing ewes suffer most because they have fewer body reserves. Both scab and lice tend to build up in the cooler, wetter months, for example the cold season in the Kenyan highlands around June to August in areas like Nyandarua, Nakuru, Laikipia, Narok and Molo, when fleeces are long and sheep are kept close together. Lice increase when nutrition is poor and sheep are stressed. Flocks that share grazing, buy animals from markets without quarantine, use communal dips with poor dip strength, or have not been sheared for a long time are at higher risk.

early: Sheep rub against posts, walls, trees or each other more than usual, and you see tufts of wool caught on fences and bushes.
Sheep turn round to bite or nibble their own sides, shoulders or flanks, or scratch with a hind foot.
The fleece looks slightly raised, open or ragged in small patches, often first over the shoulders, back and sides for scab.
When you part the wool at the edge of a damaged patch with scab, the skin is red and moist, with small pale yellow crusts.
For lice, when you part the wool in good light you can see tiny pale-brown moving insects about 1 to 2 millimetres long, or their eggs (nits) stuck to the wool fibres.
When you scratch or rub an itchy patch, the sheep may stretch its neck, lick its lips and make nibbling movements with its mouth, called the nibble reflex.
advanced: Large bare patches of skin with thick yellow or grey crusts, cracked skin and wet, smelly areas where the skin has been damaged.
The whole fleece becomes matted, stained and pulled out, and sheep may lose most of their wool.
Sheep lose weight fast, stop grazing properly because they are busy rubbing, and ewes produce less milk so lambs grow poorly.
Skin becomes thickened, wrinkled and darkened in long-standing cases.
Very badly affected sheep may be weak, lie down a lot, shiver in cold weather and in severe scab can have fits when handled, which can look like a seizure.
Heavy sucking lice burdens can cause pale gums and inner eyelids from anaemia, and weakness.
Damaged skin can become infected or attract flies, leading to fly strike (maggots in the wool).
Deaths can occur in lambs and weak sheep, especially in cold weather after losing their wool.

lookalikes.name: Sheep keds (Melophagus ovinus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Keds are wingless flies about 4 to 7 millimetres long, much bigger than lice, reddish-brown, with six strong legs, and easy to see when you part the wool. They cause rubbing and stained wool but do not cause the wet yellow crusty spreading sores of scab.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (lumpy wool)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a bacterial skin infection that forms hard crusts which bind wool fibres into lumps along the back, often after long wet spells. It causes much less itching than scab, and the scabs lift off as hard clumps of wool with a moist base, without the intense rubbing and biting.

lookalikes.name: Sarcoptic or chorioptic mange
lookalikes.howToTell: Sarcoptic mange mainly affects the face, ears and other areas with little wool, and chorioptic mange mainly the lower legs and scrotum. Psoroptic scab usually starts on the woolly areas of the body such as the shoulders, back and sides. A vet's skin scraping identifies which mite it is.

lookalikes.name: Photosensitisation or fly strike
lookalikes.howToTell: Photosensitisation causes swelling, redness and peeling on pale, sun-exposed areas like the ears, face and eyelids after eating certain plants or with liver damage, not spreading crusts in the fleece. Fly strike shows maggots, a foul smell and wet, discoloured wool, usually around the tail, back end or wounds.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer will first watch the flock for rubbing and biting, then handle several sheep, part the wool and look closely at damaged areas. For lice, they part the wool in about ten places on each side of several sheep and count the lice they see, which also shows how heavy the infestation is. For scab, they take a skin scraping from the moist edge of a fresh sore, where live mites gather, and look at it under a microscope to see the mites and identify them as Psoroptes. Because mites can be hard to find, several scrapings from several sheep may be needed, and a negative result does not always mean the sheep is free. In some countries a blood test can detect scab exposure, but this is not widely available in Kenya. To help, keep the itchy sheep penned so they can be examined, note when the problem started, which sheep are affected, any new animals bought in, and what dips or drugs have been used recently and when.
firstSteps: Separate the sheep that are rubbing and biting into their own pen, away from the main flock, goats and any newly bought animals.
Stop selling, buying, lending rams or mixing your sheep with other flocks until you know what the problem is and it has been treated.
Check every sheep in the flock by parting the wool in several places, and write down how many are affected and where on the body.
Give the affected sheep clean water, good feed and shelter from cold wind and rain, especially any that have lost a lot of wool.
Wear gloves and wash your hands and arms after handling itchy sheep, and wash clothes, as mites and lice can be carried on clothing to other sheep.
Do not buy or apply a dip, pour-on or injection before the vet has confirmed whether it is scab or lice, because the right product is different for each.
Remove wool tufts from fences and posts and burn them, and avoid putting clean sheep in pens used by affected sheep for at least two to three weeks.
Call your vet, animal health officer or County Veterinary Office, and tell your neighbours who share grazing or water so they can check their flocks too.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on whether the problem is scab, lice or both, and it must be chosen and prescribed by a vet. For sheep scab, vets commonly use injectable macrocyclic lactones, such as ivermectin, doramectin or moxidectin, or a proper plunge dip with a product licensed for scab, such as some organophosphate dips. Injections may need repeating to break the mite life cycle, and they do not prevent reinfection unless the whole flock is treated and contact with untreated sheep stops. For lice, vets often recommend dips, sprays or pour-ons containing synthetic pyrethroids such as cypermethrin or deltamethrin, or insect growth regulators, usually applied soon after shearing. Many lice pour-ons do not control scab, and most injectable products do not control chewing lice well, so using the wrong one wastes money. The most important rule is to treat every sheep in the flock on the same day, and any goats in contact if the vet advises, not just the itchy ones. Dips must be mixed at the correct strength and sheep kept in long enough for the chemical to soak through the fleece, which spraying with a knapsack often fails to do. Resistance to some products is reported in other countries, so if itching continues after treatment, tell your vet instead of repeating the same product. Sheep with infected sores or fly strike may need wound care and, only where a vet judges it necessary, antibiotics, used exactly as prescribed to limit antimicrobial resistance. All these drugs have meat and milk withdrawal periods, which are the days you must wait after treatment before slaughtering or using milk. Some injectable products have long withdrawal periods, so follow the label and the vet's advice strictly. Itching usually eases over one to three weeks, and the wool takes months to regrow.
prevention: Quarantine every new sheep, ram or goat for at least three weeks, check them carefully for rubbing and lice, and treat them as your vet advises before they join the flock.
Shear sheep at least once a year, as shearing removes many lice and makes later treatment work much better, and clean and disinfect shearing equipment between flocks.
Plan flock treatments with your vet, ideally treating all sheep at the same time after shearing for lice, and before the cold season in highland areas.
If you use a communal or private dip, make sure the dip wash is the right strength and is topped up correctly, and each sheep is fully soaked including the head.
Avoid mixing your sheep with other flocks at grazing, watering points and markets where possible, and talk with neighbours to treat at the same time so flocks do not reinfect each other.
Keep sheep in good condition with enough feed, clean water and minerals, as well-fed sheep resist lice better and recover faster.
Check the flock weekly for rubbing, wool tufts on fences and ragged fleece, and examine any suspicious sheep at once so a small problem does not become a flock outbreak.
Keep a record of every treatment, the product used, the date and the withdrawal period, so you can track what works and avoid repeating failed products.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, scab and lice cost money in several ways. Sheep spend time rubbing instead of grazing, so they lose weight and grow slowly, and ewes give less milk so lambs are lighter at weaning. Wool yield and quality drop sharply, which matters greatly for wool farmers in Nyandarua, Laikipia and other highland areas, and damaged skins fetch lower prices at tanneries. Scabby sheep look poor at the market and sell for less, and buyers may avoid a flock known to have scab. Severe scab can kill lambs and weak sheep, especially in the cold season. On top of this come the costs of dips, drugs, labour and repeated treatments if the first round fails, plus lost sales during withdrawal periods.
detail.humanHealth: The sheep scab mite Psoroptes ovis and sheep lice do not live on people. They may briefly cause mild itching on the arms of people who handle infested sheep, but this is uncommon and short-lived. The bigger human risk comes from the chemicals used to treat them. Some dips, especially organophosphates, can poison people through the skin or by breathing spray mist. Always wear gloves, long sleeves, boots and eye protection when mixing or using dips, never eat, drink or smoke while dipping, wash well afterwards, keep children away, and dispose of old dip wash safely away from rivers, wells and boreholes. Observe the meat and milk withdrawal periods on every product so residues do not reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: Most sheep recover well when the problem is identified correctly and the whole flock is treated properly with the right product. Itching eases within a few weeks and the fleece regrows over the following months, although badly damaged skin may stay thickened. Outcomes are worse for lambs, old or very thin sheep, sheep that have lost most of their wool in cold weather, and flocks where only some animals are treated or the dip is too weak. Reinfection is common if neighbouring flocks are not treated or new animals are not quarantined, so lasting success depends on flock-wide and community-wide control.

faqs.q: How can I tell sheep scab from lice on my own farm?
faqs.a: Both cause rubbing and wool loss, but they look different up close. With lice, when you part the wool in good light you see tiny moving insects and small eggs stuck to the fibres, and the skin is usually dry and scurfy. With scab, the mites are too small to see easily, but the skin at the edge of the bare patch is red and wet with yellow crusts, and the sores spread outwards quickly. Sheep with scab are usually far more itchy and distressed. A vet's skin scraping is the only way to be sure.

faqs.q: Can I just spray the sheep that are itching?
faqs.a: No. By the time a few sheep are scratching, many others are usually carrying mites or lice without showing it yet. If you treat only the itchy ones, the others reinfect them within weeks. Treat the whole flock on the same day, as your vet advises, and include in-contact goats if recommended. Knapsack spraying often does not soak through a full fleece, so dipping or a suitable vet-prescribed product usually works better.

faqs.q: I dipped my sheep but they are still scratching. What went wrong?
faqs.a: Several things can cause this. The product may control lice but not scab, or the reverse. The dip may have been too weak or the sheep not soaked long enough. Only some sheep may have been treated, or the sheep were put back into dirty pens or mixed with untreated flocks. Skin also stays itchy for a while after the parasites die. In some cases the parasites may be resistant to the product. Call your vet before treating again so they can check the cause and choose a different approach.

faqs.q: Do my hair sheep like Red Maasai or Dorper need to be checked?
faqs.a: Yes. Hair sheep usually show less dramatic wool damage, but they can still carry scab mites and lice, suffer itching and weight loss, and pass the parasites to woolly sheep and goats. Check them the same way, by parting the hair and looking at the skin, and include them in whole-flock treatment.

faqs.q: How long should I keep sheep out of a pen after an outbreak?
faqs.a: Scab mites can survive off the sheep for around two weeks, sometimes a little longer in cool, damp conditions. Keep clean or treated sheep out of contaminated pens, bomas and trucks for at least two to three weeks, or clean them thoroughly. Lice survive only a few days off the sheep, but cleaning pens and removing wool from fences still helps.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell a sheep straight after treating it for scab?
faqs.a: No. Dips, pour-ons and injections all have withdrawal periods, which are the days you must wait before the meat or milk is safe. Some injectable scab treatments have long withdrawal periods. Read the label, ask your vet or agrovet, write the safe date in your records, and do not slaughter or sell for meat before that date.

products.role: As a vet-approved supportive supplement, vitamins A, D3 and E can help sheep that have been run down by scab or heavy lice to support normal skin repair, wool regrowth and general condition during recovery. It does not kill mites or lice and must be used alongside the vet-prescribed treatment of the whole flock and good feeding.

sheep-scab.seoDescription: Sheep scab and lice in Kenya: spot rubbing, wool loss and yellow crusts early, tell scab from lice, act before the vet comes and protect your whole flock.

card.headline: Mass abortions and lamb deaths after floods
card.look: After heavy rains and flooding, many pregnant ewes abort at once and newborn lambs become weak, feverish and die within a day or two. Adult sheep may show high fever, a running nose, foul or bloody diarrhoea and weakness.
card.action: Do not touch aborted foetuses, blood or carcasses with bare hands. Isolate the flock, stop all movement and sales, and call the County Veterinary Officer immediately, because this is a notifiable disease that also infects people.

detail.summary: Rift Valley fever (RVF) is a viral disease spread mainly by mosquitoes. It breaks out after unusually heavy rains and flooding, such as during El Niño years. In sheep it causes waves of abortions, called 'abortion storms', and kills very many young lambs. It also infects people, sometimes seriously. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected case must be reported to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: RVF is caused by the Rift Valley fever virus, a virus in the Phlebovirus group. Certain floodwater mosquitoes, mainly Aedes species, lay eggs in the soil of shallow depressions and dams. Some of these eggs already carry the virus and can survive in dry ground for years. When heavy rain floods these areas, the eggs hatch in huge numbers and the infected mosquitoes bite livestock. Other mosquitoes, such as Culex, then feed on infected animals and spread the virus further, so the outbreak grows quickly. Inside the sheep, the virus multiplies fast and attacks the liver especially hard, destroying liver cells. This is why sick animals can become jaundiced (yellow gums and eyes) and bleed easily. The virus also crosses the placenta (the organ linking mother and unborn lamb) and kills the foetus, causing abortion at any stage of pregnancy. Newborn lambs have weak defences, so the virus overwhelms them within hours to a day or two.
spread: Bites from infected Aedes mosquitoes that hatch in large numbers from flooded ground after heavy or prolonged rains.
Bites from other mosquitoes, such as Culex, that pick up the virus from infected animals and pass it on, making the outbreak spread across a whole area.
Direct contact with blood, aborted foetuses, afterbirth and body fluids of infected animals can spread the virus, especially to people handling them.
Moving infected animals to markets, new grazing or other counties can carry the virus into new areas where mosquitoes then spread it.
Reusing needles between animals during an outbreak can carry the virus from one sheep to another.
Outbreaks in Kenya have been closely linked to El Niño rains and flooding, often following a long dry period.
detail.atRisk: All sheep can be infected, but newborn and very young lambs are most likely to die, and pregnant ewes are most likely to abort. Exotic and improved breeds and their crosses (such as Dorper and Merino crosses) are often hit harder than local hair sheep, but local breeds are not safe. Sheep are generally more severely affected than goats, cattle and camels, although all these can be infected. Risk is highest during and shortly after very heavy long or short rains, especially in El Niño years. In Kenya, past outbreaks have hit north-eastern and coastal counties such as Garissa, Tana River and Wajir, and parts of the Rift Valley such as Baringo, but any area with flooding, dams, swamps or irrigation schemes can be at risk. Pastoral flocks that graze near floodplains and water points, and flocks that have not been vaccinated, face the greatest danger.

early: High fever: the sheep feels hot, breathes fast and stands apart from the flock.
Loss of appetite and weakness; sheep lag behind when herded.
Newborn and young lambs stop suckling, become dull and lie down, often with a swollen or painful-looking belly.
Pregnant ewes start aborting, often several or many in a short time, at any stage of pregnancy.
Watery or blood-stained discharge from the nose.
Sudden death of young lambs, sometimes within a day of first looking unwell.
advanced: Very high numbers of lamb deaths in the flock, with most young lambs affected in a bad outbreak.
Abortion storms where a large share of pregnant ewes lose their lambs.
Foul-smelling diarrhoea that may contain blood.
Yellow colour (jaundice) in the gums, inside the eyelids and the whites of the eyes.
Bleeding signs, such as blood in the dung, from the nose or small bleeding spots on the gums.
Adult sheep that collapse, become very weak and may die, although many adults survive.

lookalikes.name: Brucellosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Brucellosis also causes abortions, but they usually happen late in pregnancy and spread slowly over months, not as a sudden storm after floods. It does not cause mass deaths of newborn lambs or high fever in adults. Both are dangerous to people, so handle all abortions with gloves.

lookalikes.name: Bluetongue
lookalikes.howToTell: Bluetongue also follows the rains because it is spread by biting midges. But it typically causes a swollen face and lips, sores in the mouth, a dark or bluish tongue, lameness and pneumonia. Mass deaths of newborn lambs and jaundice are not typical.

lookalikes.name: Nairobi sheep disease
lookalikes.howToTell: This is spread by the brown ear tick, not mosquitoes, and often follows moving sheep into tick-infested areas. It causes high fever and severe, often bloody diarrhoea in adults, and you will usually find many ticks. Abortions can occur, but the link to flooding and mass lamb deaths is weaker.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (pulpy kidney)
lookalikes.howToTell: Enterotoxaemia kills fast-growing lambs suddenly, often after a change to lush feed. It does not cause abortions in ewes or fever in adults, and it is not linked to mosquitoes. It is prevented by clostridial vaccines.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will suspect RVF from the pattern: heavy rains or floods, many mosquitoes, abortions in many ewes and many young lambs dying, sometimes along with sick cattle, goats or camels and fever cases in people nearby. Confirmation needs laboratory tests. The vet or veterinary team, wearing protective clothing, will take blood from sick and recovered animals and samples such as liver from dead lambs or aborted foetuses. Laboratories, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, test for the virus itself (for example by PCR, a test that detects the virus's genetic material) or for antibodies that show recent infection (for example by ELISA). At post-mortem the liver of young lambs is often enlarged, soft, yellowish and spotted with dead areas, but the vet should do this, not the farmer. To help, write down how many ewes have aborted, how many lambs have died and when, which animals are sick, whether you have vaccinated, and recent rain and mosquito activity. Keep carcasses and foetuses covered and away from dogs and children until the vet arrives, and do not open them yourself.
firstSteps: Protect yourself first: do not touch aborted foetuses, afterbirth, blood or dead lambs with bare hands. Use gloves or plastic bags over your hands, and wash with soap and water afterwards.
Call the County Veterinary Officer or your local veterinary office straight away and report the abortions and lamb deaths. The law requires this for a suspected RVF case.
Stop all movement: do not sell, buy, slaughter, lend or move sheep, goats, cattle or camels until the vet tells you it is safe.
Keep sick sheep apart from the rest of the flock in a shaded, dry, mosquito-reduced area, and give them clean water and good feed.
Do not slaughter or eat sick or dead animals, and do not drink raw milk from the farm. Do not give meat from dead animals to dogs.
Cover carcasses and foetuses and keep children, dogs and scavengers away until the veterinary team advises on safe burial or burning.
Reduce mosquito bites for animals and people: keep animals in at dusk where possible, sleep under treated mosquito nets, and drain standing water around the homestead where you can.
Keep a written record of dates, numbers of abortions, deaths and sick animals to share with the vet.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the RVF virus in animals. Antibiotics do not cure it, because it is a virus, not a bacterium. Treatment is supportive: keeping sick animals rested, shaded, watered and fed so their bodies can fight the infection. A vet may sometimes prescribe medicines to reduce fever or antibiotics to control secondary bacterial infections in weak animals, but this is a vet decision only. Using antibiotics without need adds to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs. Any drugs used will have milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time you must wait before milk or meat can be used, and these must be followed. In practice, the veterinary authorities focus on controlling the outbreak: confirming the disease, placing quarantine, stopping livestock movement and markets, supervising safe disposal of carcasses and aborted material, and advising on vaccination of animals not yet affected. Expect that many sick lambs will die despite care, while many adult sheep will recover over a few days to weeks. Recovered animals usually develop strong, long-lasting immunity.
prevention: Vaccinate your flock before the rains when the government or your vet issues an early warning, rather than waiting for an outbreak. In Kenya, RVF vaccine is produced locally by KEVEVAPI and is available through veterinary services and agrovets.
Ask your vet which vaccine to use and when. Some live vaccines can cause abortion or birth defects if given to pregnant ewes, so timing around the breeding season matters.
Plan breeding so that ewes are not heavily pregnant and lambs are not newborn at the height of the expected long or short rains, where your system allows.
Follow Kenya Meteorological Department and county early warnings about El Niño and heavy rains, and act on vaccination advice early.
Reduce mosquito contact: avoid grazing near flooded areas and swamps at dawn and dusk, house animals at night where possible, and drain standing water around the homestead.
Use a new or sterilised needle for each animal during any vaccination or treatment, especially when RVF is suspected in the area.
Do not buy or bring in animals from areas with an outbreak, and respect quarantine and movement bans.
Handle all abortions and births with gloves, and safely bury or burn afterbirth and dead foetuses away from water sources.
detail.impact: RVF can be devastating for a Kenyan sheep farmer. In one season a flock can lose most of its new lambs and a large share of pregnancies, which wipes out a year's income and the young stock needed to grow the flock. Sick adults lose weight and condition, and ewes that abort may be slow to breed again. Quarantines close livestock markets and slaughter slabs, so even healthy animals cannot be sold, and prices crash in affected areas. Export trade in live animals and meat from the region can be stopped for months. Families also face the cost of human illness and lost work time, because the disease spreads to people who care for animals. For pastoral communities whose wealth is in their herds, an RVF outbreak can push households into hardship for years.
detail.humanHealth: Rift Valley fever is a zoonosis, meaning it spreads from animals to people. People mostly get infected by touching blood, body fluids or tissues of infected animals, for example when assisting a birth or abortion, handling aborted foetuses, slaughtering or skinning sick animals, or cutting up meat. Drinking raw milk and being bitten by infected mosquitoes are also risks. Herders, butchers, slaughterhouse workers, vets and farm families are most exposed. Most infected people have a flu-like illness with fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, and recover within about a week. A small number develop serious disease, which can include eye damage and loss of vision, brain inflammation, or bleeding that can be fatal. Precautions: wear gloves and cover cuts when handling animals, birth materials or carcasses; never slaughter or eat sick or dead animals; boil all milk; cook meat thoroughly; sleep under treated mosquito nets and use repellents; and wash well with soap and water. Anyone on the farm who develops fever after contact with sick animals should go to a health facility quickly and tell the health worker about the animal illness.
detail.outlook: For newborn and very young lambs the outlook is poor; in a bad outbreak most may die, often within a day or two of falling ill. Pregnant ewes that are infected very often abort. Adult sheep have a better chance: many recover with rest, shade, water and good feeding, though some die, especially exotic breeds and weak animals. Recovered sheep usually become immune for life and pass some protection to their lambs through colostrum (first milk). The biggest factors in how a flock fares are whether it was vaccinated before the rains, the age and pregnancy status of the animals, breed, general body condition, and how quickly the outbreak is reported and controlled in the area.

faqs.q: A ewe aborted and her lamb looks fine to cut up. Can we eat the meat of sheep that died?
faqs.a: No. Meat, blood and organs of sheep that died or were sick during a suspected RVF outbreak can infect the people who handle and cut them. Do not slaughter, skin, sell or eat them, and do not feed them to dogs. Keep the carcass covered and let the veterinary team advise on safe burial or burning.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk from my animals during an outbreak?
faqs.a: Raw milk from infected animals can carry the virus. If you must use milk from animals that look healthy, boil it thoroughly first. Milk from sick animals should not be used at all. Follow any instructions from the veterinary and public health officers in your county.

faqs.q: Can I vaccinate my pregnant ewes?
faqs.a: Talk to your vet first. Some RVF vaccines used in Kenya are live vaccines, and these can cause abortion or birth defects in pregnant ewes. The best approach is to vaccinate the flock early, before breeding and before the expected heavy rains, so pregnant ewes are already protected. Your vet will advise on the right product and timing for your flock.

faqs.q: Why do I have to report it? I am afraid my animals will be put under quarantine.
faqs.a: RVF is a notifiable disease, so Kenyan law requires anyone who suspects it to report to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. Reporting early helps the authorities confirm the disease, warn neighbours, protect people's health and stop it spreading. Quarantine and movement restrictions mean no buying, selling or moving of animals in or out of the affected area for a period. They are hard, but they shorten the outbreak and protect your community and your future market.

faqs.q: Will Rift Valley fever come back on my farm next year?
faqs.a: RVF tends to return in waves every several years, usually after very heavy rains and floods, because infected mosquito eggs can survive in dry soil for a long time. It is not usually seen every year. Sheep that survived are generally immune, but new lambs and bought-in animals are not. Keep vaccinating as your vet advises and watch for weather warnings before each rainy season.

faqs.q: Can antibiotics or fever medicines from the agrovet cure my sheep?
faqs.a: No medicine cures the RVF virus. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, so they will not stop the disease, and using them without need wastes money and adds to drug resistance. Only a vet should decide whether any medicine is needed for comfort or secondary infections, and any drug used will have withdrawal periods for milk and meat. Good nursing, shade, water and feed, plus reporting and controlling the outbreak, matter most.
